Overview

Last week you finished Milestone 1 and sat the Mid-Term. Everything you did before it was about understanding BlueFern Trading Inc. — its assets, its network, the way attackers think, the holes a scan reveals, the malware that gets in, the response when it happens, and the cryptography that protects secrets and identities. Today we start building the defences that close those holes, and we build them where the Class 4 scan found the worst problems: at the edge of the network, on the remote and wireless connections, and in the web shop itself.

This is the last new-content lecture of CS 474. The three Thursdays of December are Research Sprints — project-work sessions with a Session Pack — and January brings the review, the showcase and the Final. So today's hour carries more than usual, and it is organized in five lessons. Lesson 1: firewalls and segmentation — what a firewall decides, the four families of firewalls, the DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet) and VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks). Lesson 2: secure remote access and wireless — VPN (Virtual Private Network) types, MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) on the VPN (Virtual Private Network), WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) and WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3), guest isolation and rogue access points. Lesson 3: web-application security — four highlights of the OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Top 10:2025, input validation, HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) everywhere, secure cookies and sessions. Lesson 4: computer security software — antivirus, EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response), IDS (Intrusion Detection System) and IPS (Intrusion Prevention System), SIEM (Security Information and Event Management), password managers and patch management, with their limits and a method to choose. Lesson 5: putting it together — the target architecture, where every control must point to a threat — and how the Research Sprints work.

Everything is applied to BlueFern: the FTP (File Transfer Protocol), SSH (Secure Shell) and MySQL ports your scan found open, the flat 192.168.10.0/24 network, the Wi-Fi password printed on the showroom wall, the remote workers on personal laptops, the shared administrator password, the web shop last patched in 2023. In Hours 2 and 3 you draw BlueFern's target architecture, write the web-shop checklist and choose the security software — Binder Part 8, due Wednesday, December 2, at 23:59.

Scope note. CS 474 is a computer-security course: it studies the machines, the software that runs on them, the networks that join them and the data they hold. Firewalls, VPNs (Virtual Private Networks), Wi-Fi settings, web defences and security software are presented so that you can configure and judge them on systems you are authorized to protect. Every attack in this hour is described at recognition level, and the five simulators run entirely inside your browser. The Legal & Ethical Notice of the schedule and the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice apply to every exercise — in particular section 7.4 (a firewall rule is a change that can cut off legitimate users) and section 7.2 (no Wi-Fi monitoring on networks shared with other people).

By the end of this hour you will be able to:

  1. Explain what a firewall decides and on which information, apply first match and implicit deny to an ordered rule list, and distinguish a packet filter, a stateful firewall, an NGFW (Next-Generation Firewall) and a WAF (Web Application Firewall).
  2. Place a DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet), a private database subnet and VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) on BlueFern's network, and write the rules between the zones.
  3. Choose between a remote-access and a site-to-site VPN (Virtual Private Network), explain why MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) belongs on the VPN (Virtual Private Network), and secure Wi-Fi with WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3), separate SSIDs (Service Set Identifiers), guest isolation and rogue-AP detection.
  4. Recognize injection, XSS (Cross-Site Scripting), authentication failures and security misconfiguration from the OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Top 10:2025, and name the control that removes each (parameterized query, output encoding, rate limiting and secure sessions, HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) with HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security), hardening, allow-list validation).
  5. State what antivirus, EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response), IDS (Intrusion Detection System) / IPS (Intrusion Prevention System), SIEM (Security Information and Event Management), password managers and patch-management tools protect and miss, and choose a set with coverage across Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover.
  6. Build a control-to-threat table that passes four traceability rules, and describe how the three Research Sprints run (Session Pack, Q&A thread, exit ticket, deadlines).
The one FACT, repeated. Your weekly work IS the project, and the project IS your exam preparation. Binder Part 8 — the target architecture with its control-to-threat table, the web-shop checklist with the corrected snippet, and the security-software selection matrix — is due Wednesday, December 2, 2026, 23:59. LO (Learning Outcome) 5, “evaluate the risks faced by a given computer system”, is assessed by asking you to map controls to risks — Part 8 is exactly that, and it is the backbone of the Final (Thursday, January 21, 2027).

Lesson 1 — Firewalls and segmentation — packet filters, stateful firewalls, NGFW (Next-Generation Firewall), WAF (Web Application Firewall), DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet) and VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks)

10 + 3 min
🖼 Slides 5–14 in the slide deck
Objective. Explain what a firewall decides and on which information, distinguish the four firewall families, and place a DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet) and VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) on BlueFern's network so that each zone talks only to the zones it needs.
10 minutes of talk + 3 minutes of activity · Schedule: Part 1 (12 min) + Visualization (4 min), compressed to 10 + 3

Lesson content

1.1 What a firewall decides, and on which information

A firewall is a system — a hardware appliance, a program on a host, or a service of a cloud provider — placed at the boundary between two or more networks. For every packet or every connection that tries to cross that boundary it takes one decision: allow or deny. The decision is taken by comparing the traffic with a list of rules written by an administrator; the list as a whole is the firewall policy. The reference document is NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy.

What can a rule look at? The basic firewall sees the five-tuple of every packet: source IP (Internet Protocol) address, destination IP (Internet Protocol) address, protocol (TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), UDP (User Datagram Protocol) or ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol)), source port and destination port — plus the interface on which the packet arrived. More advanced firewalls also see the state of the connection, the application, the user and the content; we come to them in a minute.

Two rules of evaluation hold for almost every product. First, the rules are read from top to bottom and the first rule that matches decides — the remaining rules are not consulted. Second, the list ends with implicit deny (default deny), the principle you met in Class 2: what is not explicitly allowed is refused. Order therefore matters. A broad allow placed above a specific deny makes the deny useless; such a rule is called a shadowed rule, and finding shadowed rules is part of every firewall review.

Firewalls filter in both directions. Ingress filtering controls traffic entering a zone; egress filtering controls traffic leaving it. Egress filtering is often forgotten, and it matters: a web server never needs to open connections to arbitrary addresses on the Internet, so a rule that limits its outgoing traffic to the update servers stops a compromised web server from calling the attacker back.

1.2 The packet filter — stateless

The oldest and simplest family is the packet filter, also called a stateless firewall. It examines each packet in isolation, using only the header fields of that packet. It is fast and needs very little memory, which is why it survives in router access control lists (ACL) and in the network ACLs (Access Control Lists) of cloud providers.

Its weakness comes from having no memory. When a customer's browser opens a connection to the web shop on port 443, the server's replies come back from port 443 to a random high port of the customer, between 1024 and 65535. A stateless filter cannot know that a reply belongs to a connection the customer opened, so the administrator must write a broad rule such as “allow TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) from source port 443 to any destination port from 1024 to 65535”. An attacker who forges packets with source port 443 passes that rule — towards any high port, including 3306, the port of MySQL. A packet filter also cannot see inside the packet: an attack carried in a valid web request is invisible to it.

1.3 The stateful firewall

A stateful firewall keeps a state table (also called the connection table). When a new connection is allowed by a rule, the firewall records its five-tuple and its TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) state — handshake started, established, closing. Every later packet is first compared with the state table: a packet that belongs to a recorded connection is allowed as part of it; a packet that claims to be a reply but matches no entry is dropped. Only packets that try to open a new connection are compared with the rules.

The consequence is simple: no broad “return traffic” rule is needed, and the forged source-port-443 packet of the previous section is dropped because no customer ever opened that connection. Stateful inspection is the default behaviour of modern firewalls, of the firewalls built into operating systems — Windows Defender Firewall, Linux nftables with connection tracking — and of the security groups of the major cloud providers. Its limit is the same as the packet filter's for content: it still decides by addresses, ports and connection state, and port 443 can carry anything.

1.4 The next-generation firewall (NGFW) and the UTM (Unified Threat Management)

A next-generation firewall (NGFW) adds four capabilities to stateful inspection. Application identification recognizes the application from the content of the traffic, whatever the port — a rule can allow the company's cloud e-mail and refuse file-sharing applications, both on port 443. User identity comes from the company directory, so a rule can say “finance group” instead of an IP (Internet Protocol) address. An integrated intrusion prevention engine applies the signatures you met in Class 6. URL (Uniform Resource Locator) categorization blocks categories of websites.

To see inside encrypted traffic, an NGFW (Next-Generation Firewall) can perform TLS (Transport Layer Security) inspection: it ends the encrypted session from the user, inspects the content, and opens a new encrypted session to the website, using a company certificate that the company's devices are configured to trust. TLS (Transport Layer Security) inspection has a cost in processing and in privacy, so it must be announced in the acceptable use policy and is usually excluded for banking and health websites.

A unified threat management (UTM) appliance is the older all-in-one box for small offices: firewall, antivirus, spam filter, web filter and VPN (Virtual Private Network) in one device. It is convenient; its performance drops quickly when every function is enabled.

1.5 The web application firewall (WAF)

A web application firewall (WAF) protects one kind of system — web applications — by inspecting the HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) requests and responses themselves. It recognizes the patterns of SQL (Structured Query Language) injection, cross-site scripting and path traversal inside form fields and URL (Uniform Resource Locator) parameters, limits the request rate of a client, and can apply a virtual patch: a temporary rule that blocks the exploitation of a known vulnerability while the developers correct the code. A WAF (Web Application Firewall) is deployed as a reverse proxy in front of the web server, as a module of the web server (ModSecurity, Coraza), or as a cloud service. Many of them use the open OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) CRS (Core Rule Set) rule set.

Two limits must be stated clearly. A WAF (Web Application Firewall) does not correct the application — it reduces the exposure while the code is corrected, and attackers search for encodings that the rules do not recognize. And a WAF (Web Application Firewall) produces false positives: a customer review that quotes a piece of code can be blocked. In Research Sprint 2 you will meet the payment-card standard PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard), whose version 4 requires public-facing web applications to be protected by an automated technical solution that detects and prevents web attacks — in practice, a WAF (Web Application Firewall).

1.6 Segmentation — zones, the DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet) and VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks)

Segmentation divides a network into zones, and places a firewall — or a filtering router — at every passage between zones, so that the compromise of one zone does not give access to all the others. The movement of an attacker from a first compromised machine to the next ones is called lateral movement; segmentation exists to limit it. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security describes the zones in its guidance ITSG-38: the Public Zone (the Internet), the Public Access Zone (the servers that must accept connections from the Internet), the Operations Zone (the normal staff network) and the Restricted Zone (critical servers and databases).

The Public Access Zone is the classic DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet). It holds the services that must accept connections from the Internet — web, mail, public DNS (Domain Name System) — and nothing else. Its rules are strict in three directions: from the Internet, only the published ports of the published servers; from the DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet) to the internal network, only the flows that are strictly needed, from the precise source to the precise destination; from the internal network to the DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet), administration only from a management network or through the VPN (Virtual Private Network). A DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet) is built with one firewall that has three interfaces or with two firewalls placed one behind the other.

For BlueFern, the web shop is a cloud virtual machine, so its DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet) is built in the cloud provider's network: a public subnet for the WAF (Web Application Firewall) and the web server, a private subnet for the database with no route to the Internet, and stateful security groups as the firewalls. MySQL is then reachable only from the web server, on port 3306; SSH (Secure Shell) only from the VPN (Virtual Private Network); FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is removed.

In the office, segmentation uses VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks). A VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network), standardized in IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1Q, divides one physical switch into several logical networks: each frame carries a 12-bit VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) identifier, which gives 4,094 usable VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) numbers, and devices in different VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) cannot exchange frames directly. Traffic between VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) must pass through a router or a firewall — inter-VLAN routing — and that is where the rules apply. Remember the order of cause and effect: the VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) separates; the firewall between the VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) secures. A proposed office design: VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) 10 staff, VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) 20 servers, VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) 30 the showroom POS (Point of Sale) terminal, VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) 40 the warehouse scanners, VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) 50 guests (Internet only), VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) 99 management.

In large and cloud environments, the same idea is pushed down to each server — microsegmentation — and generalized by zero trust (NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-207): no request is trusted because of the network it comes from; each one is authenticated and authorized.

Key terms of Lesson 1

TermDefinition
FirewallA system at the boundary between networks that allows or denies each packet or connection by comparing it with an ordered list of rules (the firewall policy).
Five-tupleSource IP (Internet Protocol) address, destination IP (Internet Protocol) address, protocol, source port, destination port — the fields every firewall can read.
First match / implicit denyRules are read from top to bottom and the first matching rule decides; anything not explicitly allowed is refused by the final default-deny rule.
Shadowed ruleA rule that can never take effect because a broader rule above it already matches the same traffic.
Ingress / egress filteringFiltering traffic that enters a zone / traffic that leaves it; egress filtering stops a compromised server from connecting out.
Packet filter (stateless)Examines each packet in isolation by its header fields; fast, but needs broad return-traffic rules and sees no content.
Stateful firewall / state tableRecords each allowed connection; replies are allowed only if they match a recorded connection; only new connections are checked against the rules.
Next-generation firewall (NGFW)Stateful firewall plus application identification, user identity, integrated intrusion prevention and URL (Uniform Resource Locator) categorization.
TLS (Transport Layer Security) inspectionThe firewall decrypts, inspects and re-encrypts traffic using a certificate trusted by company devices; must be announced in policy.
Unified threat management (UTM)An all-in-one appliance (firewall, antivirus, spam and web filter, VPN (Virtual Private Network)) for small offices; slows down when every function is on.
Web application firewall (WAF)Inspects HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) requests and responses to block web attacks such as SQL (Structured Query Language) injection and cross-site scripting; does not correct the application.
Virtual patchA temporary WAF (Web Application Firewall) rule that blocks exploitation of a known vulnerability until the code is corrected.
Segmentation / lateral movementDividing a network into zones with filtering between them / an attacker moving from a first compromised machine to others.
DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet)The zone for services that must accept connections from the Internet; strict rules from the Internet, to the internal network and for administration.
VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) / inter-VLAN routingA logical network on a shared switch (IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1Q, 12-bit identifier); traffic between VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) passes through a router or firewall where rules apply.
Microsegmentation / zero trustFiltering down to each workload / no implicit trust from network location; every request authenticated and authorized (NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-207).

Real-life example 1 — Closing the open ports of shop.bluefern.example — a zone design and a first-match rule set, tested packet by packet

The task of the exampleTranslate BlueFern's flat network and exposed web shop into zones (Internet, cloud DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet), cloud database subnet, office VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks)), write an ordered rule set that ends with implicit deny, and test fourteen real connection attempts against it — first as a stateless packet filter, then as a stateful firewall — to see which attempts are allowed, which are dropped, and why.
How it relates to the lectureThis is Lesson 1 applied end to end: the firewall decision and rule order (1.1), the stateless weakness (1.2) and the state table that removes it (1.3), and the zones, DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet) and VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) (1.6). The WAF (Web Application Firewall) (1.5) appears as the first hop of every customer request.

Monday morning after the Mid-Term. The two IT (Information Technology) staff of BlueFern put the Class 4 scan report on the table — vsftpd 2.3.4 on port 21, OpenSSH 7.2 on port 22 and MySQL 5.5 on port 3306, all reachable from the whole Internet — next to the Part 2 network map, and write their first real rule set. They keep the addresses they already know: the web shop's public address 203.0.113.25 (now the WAF (Web Application Firewall)), the web server 10.20.1.10 in the cloud public subnet, the database 10.20.2.10 in a new private subnet, the office VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) 192.168.10.0/24 (staff) to 192.168.50.0/24 (guests), and the VPN (Virtual Private Network) pool 10.8.0.0/24.

The rule set has nine allow rules and the final implicit deny: customers to the WAF (Web Application Firewall) on 443; WAF (Web Application Firewall) to the web server on 443; web server to the database on 3306; VPN (Virtual Private Network) administrators to the web server on 22; web server to the operating-system update servers on 443; POS (Point of Sale) terminal to the payment gateway on 443; staff to the file server on 445 (SMB (Server Message Block)); staff and guests to the Internet on 443; and — for the stateless test only — the broad return rule “source port 443 to destination ports 1024–65535”.

They then replay fourteen connection attempts captured during one hour: a customer buying boots, an Internet scanner trying 3306, 21 and 22, an administrator connecting through the VPN (Virtual Private Network), the web server calling the database and the update server, the POS (Point of Sale) terminal paying, a guest phone trying to open the file server, the web server suddenly trying to reach 198.51.100.66 on port 4444, the reply to the customer, and finally a forged packet from the Internet with source port 443, aimed at the database's port 3306.

As a packet filter, the rule set stops the scanner and the guest — and lets the forged packet reach the database, because it matches the broad return rule. As a stateful firewall, the return rule is deleted: the reply to the customer passes because it belongs to a recorded connection, and the forged packet is dropped because no such connection exists. The web server's attempt to reach port 4444 is dropped in both modes by egress filtering — that attempt is what a compromised server does when it calls back to its attacker.

Deliverable and where it goes next. The zone table, the ordered rule set and the decision log (downloadable below) are the “firewall + DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet) + VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks)” part of your target architecture in Exercise 10.1 — each rule names the threat it addresses, which is the first column of your control-to-threat table. The POS (Point of Sale) and payment-gateway rules come back in Research Sprint 2 (e-commerce review: the checkout flow and the network-control requirements of PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard)), and the before/after zone picture is a ready-made slide for the showcase of January 14.

Interactive example 1 — First-match firewall simulator — stateless versus stateful

The task of the programThe program replays fourteen connection attempts against BlueFern's ordered rule set. In packet-filter mode it compares each packet with the rules from top to bottom; in stateful mode it first looks the packet up in the state table, then evaluates the rules only for new connections and records every allowed connection. It shows the matched rule, the hit counters, the state table and the decision, and draws the packet's path between the zones.
How it relates to the lectureFirst match and implicit deny (1.1), the stateless return-traffic weakness (1.2), the state table (1.3), and the zone design with DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet), private database subnet and VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) (1.6).

File: CS474_Class10_Example1_firewall_simulator.html — self-contained HTML; a comment before every line of code; Copy · Start / Pause · Step · Restart · downloads; execution window; visualization.

Step by step — how the program works
  1. Choose the mode (Packet filter or Stateful) and press Start. The next packet appears in the execution window with its five-tuple and its source and destination zones.
  2. In stateful mode the program first searches the state table. If the packet belongs to a recorded connection (same addresses and ports, reversed), it is allowed at once — the rules are not read. The state table row flashes.
  3. Otherwise the program reads the rules from top to bottom. For each rule it compares zone, address, protocol and port; the first rule whose fields all match decides. The matched rule is highlighted and its hit counter increases.
  4. If no rule matches, the implicit deny drops the packet. The execution window prints “no rule matched → default deny”.
  5. In stateful mode, an allowed new connection is added to the state table, so that its replies pass without a rule.
  6. The canvas animates the packet from its zone to the firewall and on to its destination (green) or stops it with a red cross. Press Pause to discuss a decision; Step advances one packet; Restart clears the counters and the state table.
  7. Switch the mode and run again: packet 14 (the forged reply to port 3306) is the one that changes. Download saves the decision log (CSV (Comma-Separated Values)) and the picture (PNG (Portable Network Graphics)); Copy copies the whole program.

For each packet or connection: allow or deny, by comparing it with an ordered list of rules. A basic firewall reads the five-tuple (source and destination IP (Internet Protocol) address, protocol, source and destination port) and the arrival interface; advanced firewalls add connection state, application, user and content.
Explain “first match” and “implicit deny”.
click to reveal ↻
Rules are read from top to bottom and the first rule that matches decides; later rules are ignored. Anything that matches no rule is refused by the final default-deny rule. A broad allow above a specific deny makes the deny useless (a shadowed rule).
Stateless packet filter versus stateful firewall — the one difference and its consequence.
click to reveal ↻
The stateful firewall keeps a state table of allowed connections and accepts a reply only if it matches one. The packet filter judges each packet alone, so it needs broad return-traffic rules that forged packets (for example source port 443 to port 3306) can pass.
What is a DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet), and which three directions do its rules control?
click to reveal ↻
The zone for services that must accept connections from the Internet. Internet → DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet): only the published ports of the published servers. DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet) → internal: only strictly needed flows, precise source to precise destination. Internal → DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet): administration only from the management network or the VPN (Virtual Private Network).
Does a VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) by itself stop traffic?
click to reveal ↻
No. A VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network), standardized in IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1Q, separates devices into logical networks on a shared switch; traffic between VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) must pass through a router or firewall, and the security comes from the rules applied there.

Quiz — 4 MCQ + 2 MSQ

📝 FORMATIVE QUIZ — this quiz is not summative: it does not count toward your final grade. Nothing is recorded; use it to check your understanding.

Q1 · MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) The rule list reads: Rule 1 — allow TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) from any address to 10.20.2.10, any port. Rule 2 — deny TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) from any address to 10.20.2.10, port 3306. A packet from the Internet to 10.20.2.10 port 3306 is:

  1. Wrong — firewalls do not give priority to deny rules; the order of the list decides.
  2. Correct — rule 1 matches first, so rule 2 is never consulted; it is a shadowed rule that should be moved above rule 1.
  3. Wrong — the implicit deny applies only when no rule matches; rule 1 matches.
  4. Wrong — rule evaluation is the same in both modes for a new connection; statefulness concerns replies.
Hint: Section 1.1 — in which order are the rules read, and when does reading stop?

Q2 · MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) A stateless packet filter contains the rule “allow TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) from source port 443 to destination ports 1024–65535”. Which packet does it let through that a stateful firewall would drop?

  1. Wrong — that request is allowed by its own rule in both modes.
  2. Wrong — a genuine reply is allowed in both modes (by the return rule or by the state table).
  3. Wrong — this rule concerns source port 443; DNS (Domain Name System) uses port 53.
  4. Correct — 3306 lies inside 1024–65535, so the broad return rule matches; a stateful firewall finds no recorded connection and drops it.
Hint: Section 1.2 — what does the stateless filter not remember?

Q3 · MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) Which component can block an SQL (Structured Query Language) injection string sent inside an HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) form submission to BlueFern's web shop?

  1. Correct — the WAF (Web Application Firewall) ends the HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) session and inspects the request parameters for injection patterns.
  2. Wrong — a packet filter reads headers only, and the office router is not even on the path to the cloud shop.
  3. Wrong — a security group decides by addresses, ports and connection state, not by request content.
  4. Wrong — a VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) separates office devices; it does not inspect web requests.
Hint: Which of these reads the content of HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) requests?

Q4 · MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) Where should the web shop's MySQL database be placed in the target design?

  1. Wrong — the DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet) is exposed to the Internet; the database must never be.
  2. Wrong — mixing the customer database with staff laptops recreates the flat network.
  3. Correct — a private subnet with no Internet route, and one rule: web server → database on 3306.
  4. Wrong — exposing MySQL was one of the Critical findings of the Class 4 scan.
Hint: The DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet) is for what the Internet must reach. Must the Internet reach the database?

Q5 · MSQ (Multiple-Select Question) (3 correct answers) Which statements about a DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet) are correct?

  1. Wrong — a VPN (Virtual Private Network) is an encrypted tunnel (Lesson 2), not a zone.
  2. Correct — that is its definition.
  3. Correct — the first of the three directions.
  4. Wrong — DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet) servers are the most exposed and need patching first.
  5. Correct — the second direction; this is what limits lateral movement from a compromised web server.
  6. Wrong — internal data belongs in the Operations or Restricted Zone.
Hint: Section 1.6 lists the content of the DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet) and its rules in three directions.

Q6 · MSQ (Multiple-Select Question) (2 correct answers) Which statements about VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) are correct?

  1. Wrong — VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) do not encrypt anything.
  2. Correct — inter-VLAN routing is where the security rules live.
  3. Correct — IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1Q tagging, 4,094 usable identifiers.
  4. Wrong — without rules between VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks), traffic still flows through the router.
  5. Wrong — a WAF (Web Application Firewall) inspects web requests; a VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) is a layer-2 separation.
  6. Wrong — the point of VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) is to share one physical switch.
Hint: The VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) separates; what secures?
2

Lesson 2 — Secure remote access and wireless — VPN (Virtual Private Network) types, MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) on the VPN (Virtual Private Network), WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) and WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3), guest isolation, rogue access points

8 + 3 min
🖼 Slides 15–23 in the slide deck
Objective. Choose the right VPN (Virtual Private Network) type for a remote user and for a site, explain why MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) belongs on the VPN (Virtual Private Network), and secure a small company's Wi-Fi with WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3), separate networks, guest isolation and rogue-AP detection.
8 minutes of talk + 3 minutes of activity · Schedule: Part 2 (10 min) + Flash-cards (3 min), compressed to 8 + 3

Lesson content

2.1 What a VPN (Virtual Private Network) is, and the two types

A virtual private network (VPN) creates an encrypted and authenticated tunnel across a network that is not trusted — usually the Internet. Traffic inside the tunnel keeps its confidentiality and its integrity, and it arrives inside the company network as if the remote device were connected there. The device that ends the tunnels on the company side is the VPN (Virtual Private Network) gateway, also called a VPN (Virtual Private Network) concentrator.

There are two types. A remote-access VPN (Virtual Private Network) connects one user's device to the company gateway — the salesperson at home, the developer in a café. A site-to-site VPN (Virtual Private Network) connects two networks permanently, gateway to gateway — for BlueFern, the office network to the cloud network where the web shop runs. Three protocol families are in use. IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) is the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) standard (architecture in RFC (Request for Comments — an Internet standards document) 4301): the IKEv2 (Internet Key Exchange version 2) protocol (RFC (Request for Comments — an Internet standards document) 7296) authenticates the two ends and negotiates the keys, and ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) encrypts each packet; tunnel mode is the usual choice for site-to-site links, and NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-77 Rev. 1 is the guide. TLS (Transport Layer Security) VPNs (Virtual Private Networks) reuse the TLS (Transport Layer Security) of Class 7, usually on port 443, which passes almost every network; they dominate remote access. WireGuard is a newer protocol with a deliberately small code base.

Two configuration choices matter. In a full tunnel, all the device's traffic goes through the VPN (Virtual Private Network), so the company's filtering and logging apply; in a split tunnel, only company traffic does, and the rest goes directly to the Internet. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, in ITSAP (IT Security Awareness Publication of the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security).80.101, advises avoiding split tunnelling as much as possible. Finally, a newer alternative to the VPN (Virtual Private Network) is zero trust network access (ZTNA): instead of placing the device inside the network, it gives access to one application at a time, after checking the user and the device — the zero-trust principle of Lesson 1, often delivered as part of a SASE (Secure Access Service Edge) cloud service.

2.2 MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) on the VPN (Virtual Private Network), and the device that connects

The VPN (Virtual Private Network) gateway is reachable from the entire Internet by design. If a password alone opens it, the attacker needs only a password — and Class 3 showed how cheaply passwords are obtained: credential stuffing with lists from other breaches, phishing, guessing. ITSAP (IT Security Awareness Publication of the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security).80.101 therefore asks for MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) on the VPN (Virtual Private Network), with phishing-resistant factors, and for the gateway itself to be kept patched — VPN (Virtual Private Network) appliances appear regularly in the lists of vulnerabilities exploited in real attacks.

Phishing-resistant MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) means a factor that an attacker cannot relay from a fake website: a FIDO2 (Fast IDentity Online 2) security key or passkey is cryptographically bound to the real site's name, so it does not answer a look-alike site. A push notification is weaker: an attacker who has the password can send prompt after prompt until a tired user approves one — this is called MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) fatigue. Number matching, where the user must type a number shown on the login screen into the phone, removes accidental approvals. The current United States guideline for authenticators is NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-63B-4 (July 2025).

The gateway can also check the device before it lets the user in — a posture check, performed by the VPN (Virtual Private Network) client or by a network access control (NAC) system: is the laptop company-managed, is its disk encrypted, are its patches current, is the endpoint protection running? Appendix A says that half of BlueFern's remote workers use personal laptops without the VPN (Virtual Private Network). A sound rule: company laptops with an always-on VPN (Virtual Private Network) reach the internal shares; personal devices reach only web applications such as webmail — or nothing.

2.3 Wi-Fi security — WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) and WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3)

WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2), available since 2004, encrypts Wi-Fi traffic with AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) in CCMP (Counter Mode with Cipher Block Chaining Message Authentication Code Protocol) mode. In its Personal mode, every device uses the same pre-shared key (PSK) — the Wi-Fi password. Two problems follow. Anyone who knows the password can join. And an attacker who records the four-message handshake of a device joining the network can test candidate passwords offline, at full speed, with no further contact with the network — so the strength of the network equals the strength of the password. Worse, with a shared PSK (Pre-Shared Key), a person who knows the password and records a handshake can derive the keys of that session and decrypt it. In its Enterprise mode, WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) uses IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 802.1X with EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) and a RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) server: each user or device has its own credentials — a certificate, or a username and password — so the access of one person who leaves the company can be removed without changing anything for the others.

WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3), introduced by the Wi-Fi Alliance in 2018 and now mandatory for Wi-Fi CERTIFIED devices, changes the Personal mode at its root. It replaces the PSK (Pre-Shared Key) handshake with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals), a key exchange that gives no material for an offline password-guessing attack and gives each session its own independent key, so knowing the password does not let a listener decrypt other people's sessions. WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3) also requires protected management frames (PMF), which stop the forged disconnection frames that attackers use to force devices off a network, and it refuses the legacy protocols WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) and TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol). For guest networks, Wi-Fi Enhanced Open, based on OWE (Opportunistic Wireless Encryption), encrypts each guest's traffic without any password — but it authenticates nobody. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-153 is the guide for securing enterprise wireless networks.

2.4 Separate networks and guest isolation

A Wi-Fi network name is an SSID (Service Set Identifier). The rule is one SSID (Service Set Identifier) per level of trust, each mapped to its own VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) from Lesson 1, with the firewall between the VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) deciding what each may reach. For BlueFern: BlueFern-Staff — WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3) Enterprise with 802.1X → VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) 10; BlueFern-Scan for the six warehouse scanners — Enterprise mode with device certificates → VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) 40, allowed to reach only the inventory application; BlueFern-Guest — WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3) Personal with a weekly-rotated password, or Enhanced Open → VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) 50, Internet only, with client isolation so that guest devices cannot reach one another.

Now we can say precisely why the password printed on the showroom wall is a problem. Today, one SSID (Service Set Identifier) serves staff, scanners and visitors; its password is visible to every visitor and readable through the window. Whoever reads it joins the same flat network as the file server and the POS (Point of Sale) terminal, and — with a shared WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) password — can decrypt the sessions of others whose handshakes are recorded. The password is not secret, and the network behind it is not separated: two weaknesses, two different controls (WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3) and separate SSIDs (Service Set Identifiers) on separate VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks)).

2.5 Rogue access points

A rogue access point is an AP (Access Point) connected to, or imitating, the company network without authorization. Two forms matter. The first is the travel router that an employee plugs into an office wall socket for convenience: it creates an unprotected entry point into the internal network. The second is the evil twin: an attacker's AP (Access Point) that broadcasts the company's SSID (Service Set Identifier), so that devices connect to it and send their traffic — or their passwords — through the attacker's equipment.

Three measures detect or prevent them. A wireless survey — periodic, with a survey tool, or continuous, with a WIDS (Wireless Intrusion Detection System) or WIPS (Wireless Intrusion Prevention System) — compares every observed beacon with the inventory of authorized APs (Access Points): their BSSID (Basic Service Set Identifier), which is the MAC (Media Access Control) address of each AP (Access Point), their security mode and their channel; an unknown BSSID (Basic Service Set Identifier) announcing the company's SSID (Service Set Identifier), or a company SSID (Service Set Identifier) announced without encryption, raises an alert, and the signal strength helps locate it. On the wired side, 802.1X on switch ports refuses an unknown device plugged into a wall socket. And on the devices, Enterprise Wi-Fi must be configured to verify the RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) server's certificate, so that a laptop never sends its credentials to an evil twin. One legal reminder: surveying is done only on networks you own or are authorized to monitor — Legal Notice section 7.2 forbids monitor mode on a network shared with other people.

Key terms of Lesson 2

TermDefinition
Virtual private network (VPN)An encrypted, authenticated tunnel across an untrusted network that makes a remote device or network appear inside the company network.
Remote-access VPN (Virtual Private Network) / site-to-site VPN (Virtual Private Network)One user's device to the company gateway / two networks connected permanently, gateway to gateway.
VPN (Virtual Private Network) gateway (concentrator)The device that ends the VPN (Virtual Private Network) tunnels on the company side; reachable from the Internet, so it must be patched and protected by MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication).
IPsec (Internet Protocol Security), IKEv2 (Internet Key Exchange version 2), ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload)The IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) VPN (Virtual Private Network) suite: IKEv2 (Internet Key Exchange version 2) authenticates the ends and negotiates keys; ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) encrypts each packet; tunnel mode for site-to-site links.
TLS (Transport Layer Security) VPN (Virtual Private Network) / WireGuardA VPN (Virtual Private Network) built on TLS (Transport Layer Security), usually on port 443 / a newer VPN (Virtual Private Network) protocol with a small code base.
Full tunnel / split tunnelAll traffic through the VPN (Virtual Private Network) / only company traffic through it; the Canadian Centre advises avoiding split tunnelling.
Zero trust network access (ZTNA)Access to one application at a time after checking user and device, instead of placing the device inside the network.
Phishing-resistant MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication)A factor that cannot be relayed from a fake site, such as a FIDO2 (Fast IDentity Online 2) security key or passkey bound to the real site's name.
MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) fatigue / number matchingRepeated push prompts until a user approves one / the user must type a number shown on the login screen, which removes accidental approvals.
Posture check / NAC (Network Access Control)Verifying the device (managed, encrypted, patched, protected) before granting network access.
WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) Personal (PSK (Pre-Shared Key)) / Enterprise (802.1X)One shared password for all devices / individual credentials checked by a RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) server through EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol).
WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3), SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals), PMF (Protected Management Frames)Current Wi-Fi security: SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) resists offline password guessing and gives each session its own key; PMF (Protected Management Frames) stops forged disconnection frames; legacy WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) and TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol) refused.
Wi-Fi Enhanced Open (OWE (Opportunistic Wireless Encryption))Encryption for open guest networks without a password; no authentication.
SSID (Service Set Identifier) / BSSID (Basic Service Set Identifier)The network name / the MAC (Media Access Control) address of one access point announcing that name.
Client isolationPrevents devices on the same Wi-Fi network (for example, guests) from communicating with each other.
Rogue AP (Access Point) / evil twinAn unauthorized access point connected to or imitating the company network / an attacker's AP (Access Point) that broadcasts the company's SSID (Service Set Identifier).
WIDS (Wireless Intrusion Detection System) / WIPS (Wireless Intrusion Prevention System) / wireless surveySystems and procedures that compare observed beacons with the inventory of authorized APs (Access Points) to detect, locate and contain rogue APs (Access Points).

Real-life example 2 — The password on the showroom wall — BlueFern's Wi-Fi and remote-access redesign, event by event

The task of the exampleReplace BlueFern's single shared SSID (Service Set Identifier) and optional VPN (Virtual Private Network) with three SSIDs (Service Set Identifiers) mapped to VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks), WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3), guest isolation, a rogue-AP check, and a VPN (Virtual Private Network) that requires MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) and a managed device — then replay twelve real connection events of one working day against the new policy and record, for each, the decision and the reason.
How it relates to the lectureVPN (Virtual Private Network) types and tunnels (2.1), MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) and posture checks (2.2), WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) versus WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3) (2.3), separate networks and guest isolation (2.4), and rogue-AP detection (2.5) — each event exercises one of them.

Tuesday. The new design has been live for one day. At 07:55 a warehouse scanner joins BlueFern-Scan with its device certificate and lands in VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) 40, where it can reach the inventory application and nothing else. At 08:02 a sales laptop joins BlueFern-Staff with 802.1X and lands in VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) 10. At 08:30 a visitor's phone joins BlueFern-Guest with this week's password — shown on the reception screen, no longer painted on the wall — and lands in VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) 50; one minute later the same phone tries to open the file server at 192.168.20.10 on port 445 and is refused by the guest rule (Internet only).

At 09:10 the wireless survey reports a beacon announcing “BlueFern-Staff” from an unknown BSSID (Basic Service Set Identifier), with no encryption, at −38 dBm near the showroom entrance: an evil twin, or a rogue AP (Access Point). At 09:12 an IT (Information Technology) staff member walks the floor with the signal strength and finds a travel router plugged into a showroom wall socket; the switch port is disabled, and 802.1X on the switch ports will refuse the next one.

At 10:05 a remote worker on a company laptop opens the VPN (Virtual Private Network): password correct, number-matching prompt approved, posture check passed — a full tunnel is established and the file share is reachable. At 10:40 an attacker tries the same worker's password, taken from the 2023 breach of an unrelated shopping site: the password is correct, but no prompt is approved — access denied. From 10:41 to 10:44 the attacker sends prompt after prompt; after three refusals the account is locked and an alert goes to the log collector — MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) fatigue does not work against number matching and a lockout. At 11:20 another remote worker connects from a personal laptop: the posture check fails, and the access is limited to webmail. At 13:15 an old handheld that supports only WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) with TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol) is refused by the WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3) network; it goes on the replacement list. At 16:00 the guest password rotates automatically for the next week.

Deliverable and where it goes next. The SSID (Service Set Identifier) plan (SSID (Service Set Identifier) · security mode · authentication · VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) · allowed destinations), the remote-access rule and the event log (downloadable below) give you the “VPN (Virtual Private Network) with MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication)” and “guest Wi-Fi isolation” boxes of Exercise 10.1, each with the threat it addresses. In Research Sprint 2 (insider threat and data leakage), the leaver procedure starts here: removing one person's 802.1X credential and VPN (Virtual Private Network) access is the joiner/mover/leaver step for this part of the network; the separation of the POS (Point of Sale) terminal is checked again in the e-commerce review.

Interactive example 2 — Wi-Fi and remote-access policy checker

The task of the programThe program replays twelve events of one working day — devices joining SSIDs (Service Set Identifiers), a guest reaching for the file server, a rogue AP (Access Point) appearing, remote VPN (Virtual Private Network) logins with and without MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication), a personal laptop, a legacy device — and evaluates each against BlueFern's new policy. It shows the decision, the rule that produced it and the reason, draws the event on a floor plan (showroom, office, warehouse, the Internet and the VPN (Virtual Private Network) gateway), and keeps counters of allowed, denied and alerted events.
How it relates to the lectureThe VPN (Virtual Private Network) types and the full tunnel (2.1), MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication), number matching, lockout and posture checks (2.2), WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3) versus legacy security (2.3), SSIDs (Service Set Identifiers) mapped to VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) and guest isolation (2.4), and rogue-AP detection by comparison with the inventory of authorized BSSIDs (Basic Service Set Identifiers) (2.5).

File: CS474_Class10_Example2_wifi_vpn_policy.html — self-contained HTML; a comment before every line of code; Copy · Start / Pause · Step · Restart · downloads; execution window; visualization.

Step by step — how the program works
  1. Press Start. The next event appears with its time, the device, and what the device is trying to do.
  2. For a Wi-Fi event, the program checks the SSID (Service Set Identifier) against the policy table: required security mode (WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3) or the allowed Enterprise mode), authentication method (802.1X, device certificate or rotating password) and target VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network).
  3. For a reachability event, it applies the VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) rules of Lesson 1: guests to the Internet only, scanners to the inventory application only.
  4. For a survey event, it compares the observed BSSID (Basic Service Set Identifier), SSID (Service Set Identifier) and security mode with the inventory of authorized APs (Access Points); a mismatch raises a rogue-AP alert, drawn as a red pulse at the measured position.
  5. For a VPN (Virtual Private Network) event, it checks in order: password, MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) approval (with number matching and a three-refusal lockout), and posture (managed device, disk encryption, patches). The first failed check decides.
  6. The decision panel shows Allowed / Denied / Alert with the rule and the reason; the counters update. Press Pause to discuss; Step advances one event; Restart starts the day again.
  7. Download saves the event log (CSV (Comma-Separated Values)) and the floor-plan picture (PNG (Portable Network Graphics)); Copy copies the whole program.

Five flash-cards — click a card to reveal its back

Remote-access VPN (Virtual Private Network) versus site-to-site VPN (Virtual Private Network).
click to reveal ↻
Remote-access: one user's device to the company VPN (Virtual Private Network) gateway (salesperson at home). Site-to-site: two networks joined permanently, gateway to gateway (BlueFern's office to its cloud network), usually with IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) in tunnel mode.
Full tunnel versus split tunnel — and what the Canadian Centre recommends.
click to reveal ↻
Full tunnel: all traffic through the VPN (Virtual Private Network), so company filtering and logging apply. Split tunnel: only company traffic through it. ITSAP (IT Security Awareness Publication of the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security).80.101 advises avoiding split tunnelling as much as possible (forced VPN (Virtual Private Network)).
Why put MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) on the VPN (Virtual Private Network), and what is MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) fatigue?
click to reveal ↻
The gateway is reachable from the whole Internet, and passwords are obtained by credential stuffing and phishing. MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) fatigue: the attacker sends push prompts repeatedly until a user approves one; number matching, lockouts and phishing-resistant factors (FIDO2 (Fast IDentity Online 2), passkeys) defeat it.
WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) Personal versus WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3) Personal — what changes with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals)?
click to reveal ↻
WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) Personal uses one shared key: a recorded handshake allows offline password guessing, and anyone with the password can decrypt recorded sessions. WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3)'s SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) gives no offline-guessing material and an independent key per session; WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3) also requires PMF (Protected Management Frames) and refuses WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) and TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol).
What is a rogue AP (Access Point) or evil twin, and how is it detected or prevented?
click to reveal ↻
An unauthorized AP (Access Point) connected to or imitating the company network (a plugged-in travel router, or an attacker's AP (Access Point) broadcasting the company SSID (Service Set Identifier)). Detect: wireless survey or WIDS (Wireless Intrusion Detection System) / WIPS (Wireless Intrusion Prevention System) comparing BSSID (Basic Service Set Identifier), SSID (Service Set Identifier) and security mode with the AP (Access Point) inventory. Prevent: 802.1X on switch ports and devices that verify the RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) server certificate.

Quiz — 4 MCQ + 2 MSQ

📝 FORMATIVE QUIZ — this quiz is not summative: it does not count toward your final grade. Nothing is recorded; use it to check your understanding.

Q1 · MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) BlueFern's office must be connected permanently to the cloud network where the web shop runs. Which solution fits?

  1. Wrong — remote-access VPNs (Virtual Private Networks) connect individual devices, and only while they are connected.
  2. Wrong — a guest SSID (Service Set Identifier) is a Wi-Fi network; it does not join two sites.
  3. Wrong — split tunnelling is a client setting; it does not connect the office to the cloud.
  4. Correct — a site-to-site VPN (Virtual Private Network) (usually IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) in tunnel mode) joins the two networks permanently.
Hint: Two networks, permanently, gateway to gateway.

Q2 · MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) Why can a visitor who knows a shared WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) Personal password read other users' traffic?

  1. Wrong — WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) encrypts with AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) (CCMP (Counter Mode with Cipher Block Chaining Message Authentication Code Protocol)).
  2. Wrong — the password itself is never transmitted.
  3. Correct — the session keys derive from the shared key and values exchanged in the handshake; SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) in WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3) removes this.
  4. Wrong — WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) uses AES (Advanced Encryption Standard), not DES.
Hint: Section 2.3 — what does the shared key let a listener compute?

Q3 · MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) An attacker has a remote worker's correct password, taken from a breach of another website. What stops the VPN (Virtual Private Network) login?

  1. Wrong — split tunnelling concerns which traffic uses the tunnel after login, and it weakens security.
  2. Correct — the attacker does not hold the worker's phone or security key; number matching defeats repeated prompts.
  3. Wrong — the office Wi-Fi is not involved in a remote VPN (Virtual Private Network) login.
  4. Wrong — VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) separate office networks; they do not authenticate VPN (Virtual Private Network) users.
Hint: The password is correct. What second proof does the attacker not have?

Q4 · MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) The survey sees “BlueFern-Staff” announced by an unknown BSSID (Basic Service Set Identifier), with no encryption, at the strongest signal near the entrance. What is it most likely to be?

  1. Correct — an unknown BSSID (Basic Service Set Identifier) announcing the company SSID (Service Set Identifier) without encryption matches the definition of an evil twin.
  2. Wrong — a firmware update does not change the BSSID (Basic Service Set Identifier) or remove the encryption of the staff network.
  3. Wrong — the guest network has its own SSID (Service Set Identifier) and encryption.
  4. Wrong — a VPN (Virtual Private Network) gateway does not broadcast Wi-Fi beacons.
Hint: Compare with the inventory: BSSID (Basic Service Set Identifier), SSID (Service Set Identifier), security mode.

Q5 · MSQ (Multiple-Select Question) (3 correct answers) Which are features of WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3)?

  1. Wrong — encryption of the radio link does not separate trust levels; VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) and rules still do.
  2. Correct — WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3) networks disallow outdated legacy protocols.
  3. Wrong — WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3) Personal still uses a password (Enhanced Open is the password-free option, without authentication).
  4. Correct — PMF (Protected Management Frames) stops forged disconnection frames.
  5. Wrong — WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) is refused.
  6. Correct — SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) replaces the PSK (Pre-Shared Key) handshake.
Hint: Section 2.3 lists three changes.

Q6 · MSQ (Multiple-Select Question) (2 correct answers) Which statements describe a correctly built guest network for BlueFern?

  1. Wrong — a rotating password shown on a screen replaces the permanent printed one.
  2. Wrong — that recreates the flat network.
  3. Wrong — staff use 802.1X; sharing secrets between trust levels defeats the separation.
  4. Correct — client isolation protects guests from each other.
  5. Correct — separation by VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) plus a rule is what keeps guests away from internal systems.
  6. Wrong — the POS (Point of Sale) terminal must be the most isolated system of the office.
Hint: Section 2.4 — separation and isolation.
3

Lesson 3 — Web-application security essentials — OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Top 10:2025 highlights, input validation, HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) everywhere, secure cookies and sessions

12 + 4 min
🖼 Slides 24–33 in the slide deck
Objective. Recognize injection, cross-site scripting, authentication failures and security misconfiguration in a web shop, and name the control that removes each: parameterized queries, input validation, output encoding, HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) with HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security), secure cookies and sessions, and a hardened configuration.
12 minutes of talk + 4 minutes of activity · Schedule: Part 3 (14 min) + Short practical (5 min), compressed to 12 + 4

Lesson content

3.1 Why the web shop is different, and the OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Top 10:2025

Of all BlueFern's systems, the web shop is the only one that the whole Internet is supposed to reach — every customer, and therefore every attacker. The firewalls of Lesson 1 must allow port 443 to it, so an attack that travels inside a valid HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) request passes every firewall that does not read requests. From that point, only two things can tell good input from bad: the WAF (Web Application Firewall) in front of the application, and the application itself.

OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) is a non-profit foundation that publishes free application-security standards, tools and documents. Its best-known document, the OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Top 10, is an awareness document that ranks the ten most critical categories of web-application risk, built from data contributed by testing organizations and from a community survey. The current edition, the eighth, is the OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Top 10:2025: A01 Broken Access Control, A02 Security Misconfiguration, A03 Software Supply Chain Failures, A04 Cryptographic Failures, A05 Injection, A06 Insecure Design, A07 Authentication Failures, A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures, A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures, A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions.

Today we take four highlights, with one example each: injection, cross-site scripting — which OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) counts inside the injection category — authentication failures, and security misconfiguration. One remark on names: your schedule says “broken authentication”, which was the title of this category in 2017; in 2021 it became “Identification and Authentication Failures”, and in 2025 “Authentication Failures”. The OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) handout carries the other categories.

3.2 Injection (A05:2025) — when data becomes code

Injection happens when untrusted input is pasted into a command or a query that an interpreter — an SQL (Structured Query Language) database, an operating-system shell, a directory server — then executes. The input is supposed to be a value; because it is pasted into the text of the command, it can change the structure of the command instead.

Take the search box of the web shop — not the login page, which is your practical in four minutes and your Exercise 10.2 this afternoon. The developers wrote the query by concatenation:

query = "SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%" + q + "%'"

With q = boots, the database runs the intended search. With q = x' UNION SELECT email, password_hash FROM customers --, the first quote closes the string, UNION adds a second query, and the two dashes turn the rest of the line into a comment: the result page now lists customer e-mail addresses and password hashes. You need to recognize this pattern, not to practise it — and never on a real website.

The correction is the parameterized query, also called a prepared statement. The text of the query is fixed in advance with a placeholder, ... WHERE name LIKE ?, and the value is sent to the database separately. The database has already parsed the query before it receives the value, so the value can never become SQL (Structured Query Language): x' UNION SELECT ... is simply searched as a product name and finds nothing. Two further layers come with it: allow-list input validation (Section 3.7), and a least-privilege database account — the account the web shop uses should not be able to read tables it has no business with. The OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) SQL (Structured Query Language) Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet names parameterized queries and allow-list validation as the primary defences, and calls manual escaping strongly discouraged.

3.3 Cross-site scripting (XSS) — when data becomes code in the browser

Cross-site scripting (XSS) is injection that executes in the visitor's browser. The application includes untrusted input in a page without encoding it, and the browser runs that input as script, with the full rights of the website: it can read the page, act as the user, and send away any cookie that JavaScript is allowed to read. There are three forms. Stored XSS (Cross-Site Scripting): the input is saved — a product review, for instance — and served to every visitor of the page. Reflected XSS (Cross-Site Scripting): the input arrives in a link parameter and is echoed back in the response to the one person who clicked the link. DOM-based XSS (Cross-Site Scripting): the website's own JavaScript copies untrusted data into the page's DOM (Document Object Model), the structure of the page that scripts read and change.

At BlueFern, a review that reads “Great boots” followed by a script element would run in the browser of every customer who opens that product page.

The primary defence is context-aware output encoding: before untrusted data is written into a page, the characters that have a meaning in HTML (HyperText Markup Language) are replaced by their encoded forms — < becomes &lt;, > becomes &gt;, quotes are encoded — so the browser displays the text instead of executing it. Modern web frameworks encode by default; danger comes from the functions that bypass the encoding. When users really must submit HTML (HyperText Markup Language), it passes through a maintained HTML (HyperText Markup Language) sanitizer such as DOMPurify. A Content Security Policy (CSP) header, which tells the browser which scripts it may run, is a second layer, and the HttpOnly cookie attribute (Section 3.4) keeps the session cookie out of JavaScript's reach. The OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet gives these defences in this order.

3.4 Authentication failures (A07:2025) and secure sessions

Authentication failures are the weaknesses that let an attacker log in as someone else, or stay logged in as someone else. The common ones: no protection against credential stuffing and brute force (Class 3); weak or default passwords — BlueFern's administration panel opens with the shared password BlueFern2019!; no MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) for staff and administrators; error messages that reveal whether an account exists; and weak session management.

After a successful login, the server gives the browser a session ID (Identifier), usually in a cookie, and every later request is trusted because it carries that ID (Identifier). Whoever has the ID (Identifier) is, for the server, the user. Four rules protect it. The ID (Identifier) is long and random. It is regenerated at login — otherwise an attacker who planted an ID (Identifier) in the victim's browser before the login (session fixation) is logged in with the victim. It is destroyed at logout and expires after a period of inactivity. And the cookie that carries it has the right attributes: Secure (sent only over HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure)), HttpOnly (not readable by JavaScript, which limits the damage of XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)), SameSite=Lax or Strict (not sent with requests that other websites trigger, which reduces CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)), a narrow Path and no broad Domain. The prefix __Host- in the cookie's name makes the browser enforce several of these rules. Secure and HttpOnly are defined in RFC (Request for Comments — an Internet standards document) 6265; SameSite is defined in its revision, RFC (Request for Comments — an Internet standards document) 6265bis, still an Internet-Draft but implemented by all major browsers.

On the login form itself: rate limiting and progressive delays per account and per address; checking new passwords against lists of breached passwords, as NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-63B-4 requires; MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) for every staff and administrator account; and one generic error message — “invalid username or password” — for every failure. The OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Session Management Cheat Sheet is the reference for the session rules.

3.5 HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) everywhere and HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security)

Every page of the shop — not only the login and the checkout — is served over HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure), the TLS (Transport Layer Security) protection of Class 7. A request that arrives over plain HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) receives a permanent redirect (status 301) to the HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) address. Then the server adds one response header: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains. This is HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security), defined in RFC (Request for Comments — an Internet standards document) 6797: the browser remembers, for the stated number of seconds — here one year — to contact this site only over HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure), and it converts any later HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) link to HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) before sending anything. An attacker positioned on the network path — on a café's Wi-Fi, or on BlueFern's old flat guest network — can no longer push the customer back to an unencrypted page. Certificates are renewed automatically, because an expired certificate teaches customers to click through warnings.

3.6 Security misconfiguration (A02:2025)

Security misconfiguration means that the software may be correct, but it is set up unsafely: default accounts and passwords left in place, directory listing enabled, detailed error messages and stack traces shown to visitors, services and sample applications that nobody uses, administration panels reachable from the Internet, missing security headers, configurations never reviewed. In the 2025 edition, OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) moved this category from fifth to second place.

BlueFern's shop is a catalogue of it: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) enabled “for quick uploads”, SSH (Secure Shell) and MySQL open to the Internet (Lesson 1), the administration panel at /admin opened by the shared password, a server “last patched sometime in 2023”, and an uploads folder that lists its own content — including the old export spreadsheet with names, card expiry dates and last four digits. The corrections are the hardening of Class 5 applied to the web server: a documented baseline configuration, everything not needed removed, generic error pages with the details kept in the server's log, security headers (HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security), CSP (Content Security Policy), X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff), the administration panel reachable only from the VPN (Virtual Private Network) with MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication), and a regular check of the live configuration with a dynamic scanner (DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing), Class 4).

3.7 Input validation — the principle under all of it

Every input is validated on the server. Checks in the browser are a convenience for honest users; an attacker sends requests directly and skips them. Validation uses an allow-list: for each field, the expected type, length, character set and range — an order number is “BF-” followed by six digits; a quantity is an integer from 1 to 20; a search term is at most 40 letters, digits, spaces and hyphens. Input that does not match is rejected, not repaired. A blocklist of “dangerous words” always misses an encoding.

Validation reduces what reaches the code; it does not replace parameterized queries or output encoding, because some legitimate input — an apostrophe in the name O'Brien — must still pass. That is defence in depth applied inside one application: validation, then parameterization at the database, then encoding at the output, with the WAF (Web Application Firewall) in front and the logs behind.

Key terms of Lesson 3

TermDefinition
OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Top 10:2025OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project)'s awareness document ranking the ten most critical web-application risk categories; eighth edition, 2025.
Injection (A05:2025)Untrusted input pasted into a command or query changes the command's structure; SQL (Structured Query Language) injection and XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) are its best-known forms.
Parameterized query (prepared statement)The query text is fixed with placeholders and the values are sent separately, so a value can never be parsed as SQL (Structured Query Language).
Least-privilege database accountThe application's database account can reach only the tables and operations it needs.
Cross-site scripting (XSS)Untrusted input written into a page without encoding executes as script in visitors' browsers; stored, reflected or DOM-based — when the page's own scripts write it into the DOM (Document Object Model).
Output encodingReplacing the characters that have a meaning in HTML (HyperText Markup Language) — <, > and quotes — by encoded forms before writing untrusted data into a page, for the specific context.
HTML (HyperText Markup Language) sanitizer / CSP (Content Security Policy)A maintained library that removes dangerous HTML (HyperText Markup Language) from user content / a response header that tells the browser which scripts it may run.
Authentication failures (A07:2025)Weaknesses that let an attacker log in or stay logged in as someone else: no rate limiting, weak or default passwords, no MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication), weak sessions.
Session ID (Identifier) / session fixationThe random value that identifies a logged-in browser / an attack that plants a known ID (Identifier) before login; prevented by regenerating the ID (Identifier) at login.
Secure / HttpOnly / SameSiteCookie attributes: HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) only / not readable by JavaScript / not sent with requests triggered by other websites (reduces CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)).
Rate limitingAllowing at most N login attempts per account and per address per period, with progressive delays.
HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) everywhere / HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security)Every page over TLS (Transport Layer Security) with HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) redirected / the Strict-Transport-Security header that makes the browser use only HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) for the site (RFC (Request for Comments — an Internet standards document) 6797).
Security misconfiguration (A02:2025)Correct software set up unsafely: default accounts, directory listing, verbose errors, unneeded services, exposed admin panels, missing headers.
Allow-list input validationServer-side checking of each input against its expected type, length, character set and range; non-matching input is rejected.

Micro-activity — Short practical (4 min) — find the injection, write the parameterized version

On the screen, the five lines of a login check written by concatenation (Python-style pseudocode):

u = form["user"]
p = form["pass"]
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE user = '" + u + "' AND pass = '" + p + "'"
row = db.execute(query).fetchone()
if row: login_ok()

Alone, two minutes: (1) What value of u logs in as admin without the password? (2) Rewrite line 3 and line 4 as a parameterized query. (3) One more thing is wrong with this design even after the fix — what?
