Real-life example 3 — One day of requests on shop.bluefern.example — before and after the web controls

The task of the exampleReplay twelve real HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) requests that reach the BlueFern web shop in one day — ordinary customers and attacks — through today's shop and through the shop after the controls of this lesson (HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) with HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security), WAF (Web Application Firewall), allow-list validation, parameterized queries, output encoding, secure cookies and sessions, authorization checks, hardened configuration). For each request, record the OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) 2025 category, what happens before, which control acts, and what happens after.
How it relates to the lectureEvery section of Lesson 3 appears: the Top 10:2025 categories (3.1), injection and the parameterized query (3.2), stored XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) and output encoding (3.3), credential stuffing, sessions and cookie attributes (3.4), HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) and HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) (3.5), misconfiguration (3.6) and allow-list validation (3.7).

Thursday on shop.bluefern.example. At 08:00 a customer types the address without “https”: before, the shop answers over plain HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol); after, a 301 redirect and the HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) header (A04 Cryptographic Failures). At 08:05 an ordinary search for “boots” returns twelve products in both versions — the parameterized query and the validation change nothing for honest input. At 08:12 the search field receives x' UNION SELECT email, password_hash FROM customers --: before, the result page lists customer e-mail addresses and hashes (A05 Injection); after, the WAF (Web Application Firewall) blocks the request — and if an encoding slipped past the WAF (Web Application Firewall), the validation would reject the quote, and if both failed, the parameterized query would search for a product with that strange name and find none.

At 08:40 a “review” arrives with a script element that sends document.cookie to 198.51.100.66: before, it is stored and executed for every visitor of product 77; after, output encoding displays it as text, HttpOnly keeps the session cookie unreadable, and CSP (Content Security Policy) refuses inline script (XSS (Cross-Site Scripting), inside A05). At 10:00, six hundred login attempts arrive from three hundred addresses with e-mail/password pairs from another site's breach: before, four customer accounts are taken over; after, rate limiting, breached-password checks and the lockout leave none, and the log collector receives the alert (A07 Authentication Failures). At 10:30 a real customer logs in: before, the cookie is SESSIONID=8841; Path=/ — short, predictable, no attributes, the same before and after login; after, it is __Host-SID= followed by 128 random bits, Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/, regenerated at login.

At 11:00 someone on the Internet opens /admin/: before, the shared password works; after, the panel answers 403 Forbidden outside the VPN (Virtual Private Network) (A02 Security Misconfiguration). At 11:20, /uploads/: before, a directory listing shows the file export_cards_2023.xlsx; after, listing is off and the file is deleted — data that does not exist cannot leak. At 12:00 a malformed product address makes PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) print a stack trace with file paths and the database host name: before, the visitor sees it; after, a generic error page, details in the server log only (A02, and A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions). At 13:00 a logged-in customer changes the order number in the address from 10451 (theirs) to 10452: before, another customer's name and address appear; after, the server checks that the order belongs to the session's customer and answers 404 (A01 Broken Access Control — the first category of the list, here as a bonus). At 14:00 and 15:30, two more ordinary searches pass in both versions.

Deliverable and where it goes next. The request-review table (time · request · OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) 2025 category · before · control · after), downloadable below, is the backbone of Exercise 10.2 — the 12-item web-shop security checklist and the corrected snippet. The same table, with the checkout pages added, is your starting point for the e-commerce security review of Research Sprint 2, and the before/after columns become evidence for the Final Binder.

Interactive example 3 — Web request inspector — the same request, before and after the controls

The task of the programThe program sends twelve simulated requests through two versions of the shop: “before” (today's configuration) and “after” (with the controls). For each request it walks through the defensive pipeline stage by stage — HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) and HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security), WAF (Web Application Firewall), allow-list validation, query construction, output encoding, cookies and headers, authorization and configuration — shows which stage acts, prints the query tokens in a “code versus data” view for the injection request, and records the outcome. Nothing leaves your browser: the shop, its database and its customers are JavaScript objects.
How it relates to the lectureOWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Top 10:2025 categories (3.1), the concatenated versus parameterized query (3.2), output encoding against stored XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) (3.3), rate limiting, session regeneration and cookie attributes (3.4), HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) and HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) (3.5), misconfiguration (3.6) and validation (3.7).

File: CS474_Class10_Example3_web_request_inspector.html — self-contained HTML; a comment before every line of code; Copy · Start / Pause · Step · Restart · downloads; execution window; visualization.

Step by step — how the program works
  1. Choose Before or After and press Start. The next request appears with its time, method, path and parameters, and its OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) 2025 category.
  2. The request enters the pipeline. Each stage box lights up in turn; a stage that changes the outcome turns green (it protected the shop) or red (the weakness was exploited).
  3. For the injection request, the token view shows the SQL (Structured Query Language) query as tokens: in the Before version the attacker's input becomes SQL (Structured Query Language) keywords (red tokens); in the After version the whole input stays one data token (amber) next to a fixed placeholder.
  4. For the review with a script element, the program shows the raw text and the encoded text side by side, and whether the browser would run it.
  5. For the login and session requests, it shows the Set-Cookie line and checks each attribute: Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, regeneration at login.
  6. The outcome (served normally, attack succeeded, attack stopped — by which control) is added to the review table. Press Pause to discuss; Step advances one request; Restart begins the day again.
  7. Run both versions and compare the tables. Download saves the review table (CSV (Comma-Separated Values)) and the pipeline picture (PNG (Portable Network Graphics)); Copy copies the whole program.

Five flash-cards — click a card to reveal its back

What is injection, and why does a parameterized query stop SQL (Structured Query Language) injection?
click to reveal ↻
Untrusted input pasted into a command or query changes the command's structure. A parameterized query fixes the query text with placeholders and sends the values separately; the database parses the query before it sees the value, so the value can never become SQL (Structured Query Language).
Stored versus reflected XSS (Cross-Site Scripting), and the primary defence.
click to reveal ↻
Stored: the input is saved (a review) and served to every visitor. Reflected: the input arrives in a link and is echoed to the person who clicked. Primary defence: context-aware output encoding; then sanitization for allowed HTML (HyperText Markup Language), CSP (Content Security Policy) and HttpOnly cookies as further layers.
Three cookie attributes for a session cookie, and what each does.
click to reveal ↻
Secure: sent only over HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure). HttpOnly: not readable by JavaScript (limits XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) damage). SameSite=Lax or Strict: not sent with requests triggered by other sites (reduces CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)). Also: regenerate the session ID (Identifier) at login; narrow Path; no broad Domain; __Host- prefix.
What does HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) do?
click to reveal ↻
The Strict-Transport-Security response header (RFC (Request for Comments — an Internet standards document) 6797) makes the browser remember, for max-age seconds, to contact the site only over HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) and to upgrade any HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) link before sending anything — so an attacker on the path cannot downgrade the customer to plain HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol).
Give three examples of security misconfiguration in BlueFern's shop, and the category.
click to reveal ↻
A02:2025 Security Misconfiguration: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) enabled for “quick uploads”; /admin reachable from the Internet with a shared password; directory listing of /uploads showing an export spreadsheet; stack traces shown to visitors; SSH (Secure Shell) and MySQL open to the Internet; no patching since 2023.

Quiz — 4 MCQ + 2 MSQ

📝 FORMATIVE QUIZ — this quiz is not summative: it does not count toward your final grade. Nothing is recorded; use it to check your understanding.

Q1 · MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) Which control makes the database treat the input x' UNION SELECT email, password_hash FROM customers -- as ordinary text?

  1. Wrong — HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) encrypts the request on the network; the database still receives the same concatenated query.
  2. Wrong — HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) forces HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure); it does not change how the query is built.
  3. Correct — the query is parsed before the value arrives, so the value cannot become SQL (Structured Query Language).
  4. Wrong — HttpOnly protects a cookie from JavaScript; it has nothing to do with SQL (Structured Query Language).
Hint: Section 3.2 — the database must receive the value separately from the query text.

Q2 · MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) A product review containing a script element runs in the browser of every customer who opens the page. What is it, and what is the primary fix?

  1. Wrong — reflected XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) reaches only the person who clicks a crafted link, and passwords are irrelevant here.
  2. Correct — the input is stored and served to all visitors; encoding makes the browser display it instead of running it.
  3. Wrong — the script does not attack the database; it runs in browsers.
  4. Wrong — directory listing is a different misconfiguration.
Hint: Saved and served to everyone; what turns the script into displayed text?

Q3 · MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) Which Set-Cookie line is configured correctly for a session ID (Identifier)?

  1. Correct — random value, all three attributes, the __Host- prefix and a narrow Path.
  2. Wrong — short and predictable, with no Secure, HttpOnly or SameSite attribute.
  3. Wrong — random, but a broad Domain exposes it to every subdomain and no attribute protects it.
  4. Wrong — a guessable value; Secure alone is not enough.
Hint: Section 3.4 — random, Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, narrow scope.

Q4 · MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) In the OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Top 10:2025, which category rose to second place and covers default passwords, directory listing and verbose error messages?

  1. Wrong — injection is fifth in 2025.
  2. Wrong — authentication failures are seventh and concern logging in as someone else.
  3. Wrong — A10 is new in 2025 and concerns error handling; verbose errors overlap with it, but the category that rose to second place is Security Misconfiguration.
  4. Correct — it moved from fifth (2021) to second (2025).
Hint: Section 3.6.

Q5 · MSQ (Multiple-Select Question) (3 correct answers) Which measures reduce authentication failures on the web shop's login?

  1. Correct — it prevents session fixation.
  2. Wrong — passwords are stored as salted slow hashes (Class 7) and never e-mailed.
  3. Wrong — the login page must use HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure), and HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) should enforce it.
  4. Wrong — it tells an attacker which accounts exist; use one generic message.
  5. Correct — a stolen password alone no longer opens the account.
  6. Correct — it defeats brute force and slows credential stuffing.
Hint: Section 3.4 — protect the login form and the session that follows it.

Q6 · MSQ (Multiple-Select Question) (2 correct answers) Which statements about input validation are correct?

  1. Wrong — non-matching input is rejected, not repaired.
  2. Wrong — attackers send requests directly and skip browser checks.
  3. Wrong — blocklists always miss an encoding.
  4. Correct — some legitimate input (O'Brien) must still pass, so the other layers remain necessary.
  5. Wrong — each layer covers what the others miss.
  6. Correct — server-side allow-list validation.
Hint: Section 3.7 — where, how, and what it does not replace.

Lesson 4 — Computer security software — antivirus, EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response), IDS (Intrusion Detection System) / IPS (Intrusion Prevention System), SIEM (Security Information and Event Management), password managers, patch management: capabilities, limits, how to choose

7 + 2 min
🖼 Slides 34–42 in the slide deck
Objective. State what each family of security software protects, what it cannot see, and choose a set that covers prevention, detection, response and recovery for a 38-person company with two IT (Information Technology) staff.
7 minutes of talk + 2 minutes of activity · Schedule: first part of Part 4 (10 min) + Fun quiz (3 min), compressed to 7 + 2

Lesson content

4.1 Antivirus and anti-malware

Antivirus — today usually called anti-malware — runs on each endpoint. It compares files and memory with signatures, which are byte patterns or hash values of known malware, and with heuristics, rules that score suspicious structure or behaviour. Its real-time component blocks known malware the moment a file is written or started. Modern operating systems include one, and NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-83 Rev. 1 describes its place in malware prevention.

Its limits are exactly what attackers aim at. A new or modified variant has no signature yet. A fileless attack runs in memory through scripting tools and leaves no file to scan. And an attacker who uses the administration tools already present on the machine — the practice called living off the land — gives the antivirus nothing malicious to recognize. Antivirus remains useful: it stops the large volume of known, commodity malware, including many of the tools attackers use after they get in. It is a necessary layer, not a sufficient one.

4.2 EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) and XDR (Extended Detection and Response)

Endpoint detection and response (EDR) is an agent that records, on every laptop and server, what actually happens: which process started which other process, with which command line, which files it changed, which network connections it opened. On that record it detects malicious behaviour, whatever the file: a word-processing document that starts PowerShell, a process that reads the memory of the login service, a program that renames two thousand files with encrypted content in a minute. It responds automatically — it stops the process, quarantines the file, and can isolate the host from the network while keeping its own connection to the console — which is the “isolate first” step of the Class 5 playbook, done in seconds. It also gives the investigator a timeline back to the first event. Extended detection and response (XDR) correlates the same kind of data across endpoints, e-mail, network and cloud.

The limits: EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) produces alerts that someone must examine — for a company with two IT (Information Technology) staff, a managed detection and response (MDR) service often does that work; an attacker with administrator rights may try to stop the agent, which is one more reason for the least-privilege rule of Class 5 (no local administrator rights “to install printers”); and it is licensed per endpoint.

4.3 IDS (Intrusion Detection System) / IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) and SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) — the two families from Class 6

You met both in Class 6; here is their place in a software selection. A network IDS (Intrusion Detection System) watches a copy of the traffic and alerts; an IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) sits in the path and blocks. Now that BlueFern will have VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks), the natural place for the sensor is where traffic crosses between zones — at the firewall — so that a laptop scanning the server VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) on port 445 is seen. Limits: an IDS (Intrusion Detection System) cannot read the content of encrypted traffic unless that traffic is decrypted for inspection, and it sees only the segments where it is placed.

The SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) collects the logs of everything else — firewall, VPN (Virtual Private Network), WAF (Web Application Firewall), web server, EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response), identity provider — normalizes and correlates them, and raises alerts; a SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation and Response) platform adds automated responses. Its limits are organizational: it is only as good as the logs it receives and the rules it runs, and too many low-value alerts produce alert fatigue — real alerts drown among the false ones. A SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) that nobody reads is not a control.

4.4 Password managers

A password manager stores each account's unique, randomly generated password in an encrypted vault, unlocked by one primary passphrase plus MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication). It brings three benefits. Every account gets a different strong password, so a breach of one website no longer opens the others (credential stuffing, Class 3, loses its fuel). The manager fills a password only on the exact domain where it was saved, so a look-alike phishing site such as bluefern-invoices.example receives nothing — the user notices that the autofill is silent. And a business version provides shared vaults with access control, the correct replacement for a shared administrator password such as BlueFern2019!.

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, in ITSAP (IT Security Awareness Publication of the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security).30.025, names the main risk directly: the compromise of all the accounts at once if the vault is opened. The protections are a long primary passphrase, MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) on the vault, and the vendor's encryption design. And no password manager protects a password that malware on the same laptop captures as it is typed.

4.5 Patch-management tools

A patch-management tool keeps an inventory of the software and versions on every device, downloads the vendors' updates, deploys them to a small pilot group first, then to everyone in successive deployment rings, and reports which devices are still missing which update. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-40 Rev. 4 describes patching as preventive maintenance — routine work, planned like any other, not an emergency.

Priorities come from four facts: exposure (Internet-facing systems first — the web shop, the VPN (Virtual Private Network) gateway, the firewall itself), evidence of exploitation in real attacks (such as an entry in the KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) catalogue published by CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (United States))), severity (the CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) score of Class 4) and the criticality of the asset (Class 4's multiplier). The limits: a device missing from the inventory is never patched; a zero-day has no patch yet; and end-of-life software receives no patches at all — Windows 10 reached its end of support in October 2025, and Appendix A says BlueFern runs a mix of Windows 10 and 11. End-of-life systems must be upgraded, replaced or isolated.

4.6 How to choose

Choose from the threats, not from the products. Take the threats and risks of your Binder Parts 3 and 6 and make sure that each important one has at least one control that prevents it, one that detects it, and a way to respond and recover — the functions Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover of the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework). Then compare candidates on five criteria: what it protects; what it misses; its cost class — licence, hardware and, above all, staff time; the effort to operate it (who reads its alerts, who updates its rules?); and whether it integrates — does it send its events to the SIEM (Security Information and Event Management)? For a company of 38 people with two IT (Information Technology) staff, the answer usually favours the security functions already built into the operating systems and the cloud services, centrally managed, plus a managed service for the alerts nobody has time to read.

The Canadian Centre's Baseline cyber security controls for small and medium organizations points the same way: automatically patch operating systems and applications, enable security software, use strong user authentication, establish basic perimeter defences, secure websites, back up and encrypt data. That list is your checklist for Exercise 10.3.

Key terms of Lesson 4

TermDefinition
Antivirus / anti-malwareEndpoint software that detects known malware by signatures and heuristics and blocks it in real time.
Signature / heuristicA byte pattern or hash of known malware / a rule that scores suspicious structure or behaviour.
Fileless attack / living off the landAn attack that runs in memory without a file to scan / an attack that uses the administration tools already on the machine.
Endpoint detection and response (EDR)An agent that records endpoint activity, detects malicious behaviour, responds automatically (stop, quarantine, isolate) and supports investigation.
Host isolationEDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) cuts the endpoint off the network while keeping its own console connection — the “isolate first” step, automated.
XDR (Extended Detection and Response) / MDR (Managed Detection and Response)Correlation across endpoints, e-mail, network and cloud / a managed service that examines and answers the alerts for the company.
Alert fatigueSo many low-value alerts that real ones are missed; the reason SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) rules must be tuned and owned.
Password manager / vault / primary passphraseSoftware that stores unique random passwords in an encrypted vault unlocked by one strong passphrase plus MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication); fills only on the exact domain.
Patch management / deployment ringsInventory, testing and staged deployment of updates with compliance reporting / successive groups receiving an update after a pilot group.
KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities)CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (United States))'s catalogue of vulnerabilities known to be exploited in real attacks — a strong patching priority signal.
Zero-day / end-of-lifeA vulnerability with no patch yet / software no longer receiving updates (Windows 10 since October 2025).
Coverage (Protect / Detect / Respond / Recover)Checking that each important threat has at least one control in each function of the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework).

Micro-activity — Fun quiz (2 min) — which tool for which job?

Four situations, show of hands, ten seconds each. Which family of security software is designed for it?

  1. A brand-new ransomware variant with no signature yet renames 2,000 files in one minute on a finance laptop.
  2. A laptop on the staff VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) starts connecting to port 445 of every address in the server VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network).
  3. Twelve failed VPN (Virtual Private Network) logins, then a success from another country, then a new administrator account on the file server.
  4. A salesperson uses the same password on fourteen websites.

Bonus: the web shop still runs Apache 2.4.18 from 2016.

Real-life example 4 — Friday 16:40, a new ransomware variant — what each security tool sees, stops or misses

The task of the exampleReplay one realistic intrusion against BlueFern, step by step, through eight defensive families — password manager, MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication), antivirus, EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response), patch management, network IDS (Intrusion Detection System) / IPS (Intrusion Prevention System), SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) and offline backups — switching each family on or off, to see at which step the attack is prevented, which tools only detect it, and which have no view of it at all.
How it relates to the lectureThe capabilities and limits of antivirus (4.1), EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) (4.2), IDS (Intrusion Detection System) / IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) and SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) (4.3), password managers (4.4) and patch management (4.5), and the coverage reasoning of 4.6 — the same chain seen with BlueFern's current tools and with a chosen set.

Friday afternoon. Step 0, background: fourteen attachments carrying known commodity malware reach staff mailboxes; the antivirus blocks every one by signature — that large volume of known malware is where antivirus earns its place. The targeted attack is a different story. At 16:40 a finance employee receives an e-mail that looks like a supplier invoice, with a link to bluefern-invoices.example, a look-alike of the company's cloud e-mail login page. Step 1 — phishing: with a password manager, the autofill stays silent on the wrong domain and the employee stops; without it, the password is typed into the attacker's page. Step 2 — login with the stolen password: MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) blocks it; without MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) the attacker is inside the mailbox, and only the SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) notices a login from another country. Step 3 — the macro document: from the real mailbox, the attacker sends a document with a macro to a colleague. The dropper is new, so the antivirus has no signature and misses it; EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) sees the word-processing program start PowerShell and stops it.

Step 4 — privilege escalation: the payload tries a local vulnerability published three months earlier and listed as exploited in real attacks; patch management closed it in the second deployment ring, so the attempt fails. At BlueFern today this step costs the attacker nothing — every user is already a local administrator. Step 5 — credential dumping: as administrator, the attacker first tries to switch the antivirus off, then runs a well-known password-dumping tool. Where EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response)'s tamper protection keeps the antivirus running, its signature blocks the tool and EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) blocks the memory access; without that protection, the antivirus is simply turned off — antivirus works best together with least privilege and EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response). Step 6 — lateral movement: SMB (Server Message Block) connections from the finance laptop towards the file server and twenty other laptops; the network IDS (Intrusion Detection System) at the inter-VLAN firewall raises an alert, and in IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) mode blocks them. Step 7 — encryption: the ransomware starts encrypting the shares of the file server; EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) on the server detects the mass-encryption pattern and isolates the host after 312 files instead of 48,000. Step 8 — recovery: the encrypted files come back from the offline backup copy of Class 6, and the SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) timeline gives the incident report its sequence.

With BlueFern's tools as described in Appendix A — a basic antivirus and nothing else — the commodity attachments are blocked, but the targeted attack runs from step 1 to step 7 without one alert; the first sign is the ransom note, and step 8 fails because the only backup drive is attached and encrypted too. With the full set, the attack stops at step 1. With everything except the password manager and MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication), it stops at step 3 — defence in depth means that the failure of one layer is caught by the next.

Deliverable and where it goes next. The coverage table (tool · steps it prevents · steps it detects · what it misses · cost class · effort), downloadable below, is the method of Exercise 10.3 (the security-software selection matrix: five categories × protects, misses, cost class, effort, pick for BlueFern) and gives the EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response), SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) and backup rows of the Exercise 10.1 control-to-threat table. “Which tool would you use and why, and what would it miss?” is a classic Final question (LO (Learning Outcome) 2).

Interactive example 4 — Defence-in-depth simulator — one intrusion, eight defensive families

The task of the programThe program runs the background step and the eight steps of the Friday intrusion. At each step it asks every enabled defensive family whether it can prevent, detect, or not see that step, using a capability table built from Lessons 4 and Class 6; the first family that prevents the step stops the attack, and every family that detects it raises an alert. Switches let you enable or disable each family, and presets load BlueFern's current state, the full set, and a set without identity controls.
How it relates to the lectureAntivirus signatures and their blind spot for new variants (4.1), EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) behaviour detection and host isolation (4.2), IDS (Intrusion Detection System) / IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) and SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) correlation (4.3), password-manager domain matching and MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) (4.4, Lesson 2), patch management (4.5), and coverage across Protect / Detect / Respond / Recover (4.6).

File: CS474_Class10_Example4_defense_in_depth.html — self-contained HTML; a comment before every line of code; Copy · Start / Pause · Step · Restart · downloads; execution window; visualization.

Step by step — how the program works
  1. Choose a preset (BlueFern today · Full set · No password manager / MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication)) or set the eight switches yourself, then press Start. Step 0 is background noise: commodity malware that the antivirus blocks without affecting the targeted attack.
  2. The first attack step appears on the kill-chain lane with its description, and the program evaluates every enabled family for that step.
  3. Each family's cell in the grid turns green P (prevents), amber D (detects), red ✗ (has a view of the step but misses it, such as antivirus against a new variant) or grey — (no view of this step).
  4. If a family prevents the step, the attack stops there; the damage meter freezes and the execution window prints which control stopped it. Otherwise the attack proceeds to the next step and the damage meter grows.
  5. Every detection is written to the alert list, with the step at which the first alert appeared — the earlier, the better.
  6. Press Pause to discuss a step; Step advances one step; Restart resets the attack. Change a switch and run again to compare.
  7. Download saves the coverage grid (CSV (Comma-Separated Values)) and the picture (PNG (Portable Network Graphics)); Copy copies the whole program.

Five flash-cards — click a card to reveal its back

Antivirus: how does it detect, and what does it miss?
click to reveal ↻
It compares files and memory with signatures of known malware and with heuristics, and blocks known malware in real time. It misses new or modified variants (no signature yet), fileless attacks in memory, and attackers who use the system's own administration tools (living off the land).
EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response): what does it record, detect and do?
click to reveal ↻
It records process starts, command lines, file changes and network connections on each endpoint; detects malicious behaviour (a document starting PowerShell, mass encryption); responds by stopping the process, quarantining files and isolating the host; and gives investigators a timeline.
Why does a SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) need people (or SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation and Response)), and what is alert fatigue?
click to reveal ↻
A SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) only raises alerts; someone must examine and act on them, or SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation and Response) must automate the response. Alert fatigue: so many low-value alerts that the real ones are missed — rules must be tuned and owned. A SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) nobody reads is not a control.
Password manager: two benefits and the main risk.
click to reveal ↻
Benefits: a unique random password per account (breaches stop spreading); autofill only on the exact domain (look-alike phishing sites get nothing); shared vaults replace shared admin passwords. Main risk (ITSAP (IT Security Awareness Publication of the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security).30.025): compromise of all accounts at once if the vault is opened — so a long primary passphrase and MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication).
How should patches be prioritized?
click to reveal ↻
By exposure (Internet-facing first), evidence of real exploitation (for example a KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) entry), severity (CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System)) and asset criticality. And: a device missing from the inventory is never patched; end-of-life software (Windows 10 since October 2025) must be upgraded, replaced or isolated.

Quiz — 4 MCQ + 2 MSQ

📝 FORMATIVE QUIZ — this quiz is not summative: it does not count toward your final grade. Nothing is recorded; use it to check your understanding.

Q1 · MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) A brand-new ransomware variant with no signature starts encrypting files on a laptop. Which family is designed to stop it by its behaviour?

  1. Correct — EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) detects the mass-encryption behaviour, stops the process and isolates the host.
  2. Wrong — without a signature, signature-based detection has nothing to match.
  3. Wrong — a password manager protects credentials, not files.
  4. Wrong — patching closes known vulnerabilities; it does not stop a program that is already running.
Hint: No signature exists. What watches behaviour?

Q2 · MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) Which statement describes a real limit of a network IDS (Intrusion Detection System)?

  1. Wrong — a network IDS (Intrusion Detection System) watches traffic from a sensor or mirror port, not from laptops.
  2. Wrong — it detects; the firewall enforces the zone rules.
  3. Wrong — it reports; patching is a separate process.
  4. Correct — the content of encrypted sessions is unreadable to a passive sensor.
Hint: Section 4.3 — what does a sensor on the network actually receive?

Q3 · MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) Which update should BlueFern deploy first?

  1. Wrong — internal, moderate, one device.
  2. Wrong — not a business system, and no security severity given.
  3. Correct — every priority factor points to it: exposed to the whole Internet, actively exploited, critical score.
  4. Wrong — moderate severity, internal display.
Hint: Exposure, exploitation in real attacks, severity, criticality.

Q4 · MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) Why does a password manager help against a look-alike phishing site?

  1. Wrong — password managers do not encrypt e-mail.
  2. Correct — the domain check is the phishing-resistance side benefit; the silent autofill is the warning.
  3. Wrong — that is web filtering, a different tool.
  4. Wrong — daily changes are not its function and are not recommended practice.
Hint: Section 4.4 — what does autofill compare before filling?

Q5 · MSQ (Multiple-Select Question) (3 correct answers) Which criteria belong in the choice of security software for a 38-person company?

  1. Correct — integration lets the SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) correlate.
  2. Wrong — rankings ignore the company's own risks.
  3. Wrong — price says nothing about fit.
  4. Correct — effort to operate is a criterion; an unread tool is not a control.
  5. Correct — choose from the threats, not from the products.
  6. Wrong — built-in, centrally managed features are often the best fit for small teams.
Hint: Section 4.6 — threats first, then protects / misses / cost / effort / integration.

Q6 · MSQ (Multiple-Select Question) (2 correct answers) Which statements about a SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) are correct?

  1. Correct — collection, normalization and correlation are its core.
  2. Wrong — encryption is not a SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) function.
  3. Correct — otherwise alert fatigue sets in and the alerts are not acted upon.
  4. Wrong — tuning reduces false positives; nothing removes them all.
  5. Wrong — blocking on endpoints is EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response)'s job.
  6. Wrong — antivirus runs on endpoints and matches signatures.
Hint: Section 4.3 — what it does, and what it depends on.

Lesson 5 — Putting it together — BlueFern's target architecture (controls mapped to threats) and how the Research Sprints work

5 + 4 min
🖼 Slides 43–49 in the slide deck
Objective. Assemble the controls of Lessons 1–4 into one target architecture, justify every control with a threat (control-to-threat traceability), and know exactly how the three December Research Sprints run.
5 minutes of talk + 4 minutes of activity · Schedule: second part of Part 4 (10 min) + Zen break (2 min), compressed to 5 + 4

Lesson content

5.1 Defence in depth as a design rule

Defence in depth, introduced in Class 1, is the design rule that ties today together: several independent layers of control, so that the failure of one does not become a breach. The layers are people (training, policy), process (patching, incident response, change control) and technology. Today added four technology layers to that picture — the perimeter and the zones (Lesson 1), remote and wireless access (Lesson 2), the application (Lesson 3), and the software on endpoints and in the centre (Lesson 4) — on top of the recovery layer of Class 6, the tested offline backup.

The zero-trust principle of NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-207 states the same idea from the other side: assume that some layer will fail, trust no request because of where it comes from, authenticate and authorize every access, check the device, give the least privilege, and watch everything — segmentation and monitoring are then not extra features but consequences.

5.2 From threats to controls — the traceability rules

A target architecture is two documents: a diagram of BlueFern's systems after the planned changes, with each control drawn where it acts, and a control-to-threat table that says, for each control, which threats or risks it addresses. The integration guide of Appendix B gives the rules that make the two documents trustworthy; we use four of them:

  1. No orphan control — every control points to at least one threat from Binder Part 3 or one risk from Part 6. A box with no reason is cost without benefit.
  2. No uncovered high risk — every high risk has at least one control that prevents it and at least one that detects it or recovers from it.
  3. Every control has an owner and a process — a named role and a routine: who reads the SIEM (Security Information and Event Management), who tests the restore, who approves firewall changes.
  4. The numbers agree — the asset values of Part 1, the risk register of Part 6 and the control choices of Part 8 tell the same story; a control that costs more per year than the loss it removes needs another justification.

Two example rows: “WAF (Web Application Firewall) + parameterized queries ↔ SQL (Structured Query Language) injection on the web shop (Part 3 classification, Part 4 scan)”; “EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) + offline backups ↔ ransomware on the file server (Part 6 register)”.

5.3 What goes on BlueFern's diagram

The boxes are the ones listed in Exercise 10.1, and you now know each of them: the stateful firewall with the office VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks); the DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet) for the web shop in the cloud, with the WAF (Web Application Firewall) in front and the database in a private subnet; the site-to-site VPN (Virtual Private Network) between the office and the cloud and the remote-access VPN (Virtual Private Network) with MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication); the isolated guest Wi-Fi; EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) on laptops and servers; the SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) or log collector that receives the firewall, VPN (Virtual Private Network), WAF (Web Application Firewall), web and EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) logs; patch management and the password manager; and the tested offline backups of Class 6. Placing them is your work this afternoon; tracing each one to a threat is what turns a drawing into a plan.

5.4 How the Research Sprints work — December 3, 10 and 17

The next three Thursdays are Research Sprints — supervised project-work sessions, a designed part of this project-based course. Each follows the same shape. Hour 1 is guided self-study from the Session Pack on the LMS (Learning Management System): a one-page reading guide, a 10–12-minute recorded mini-lecture or annotated slides, self-check flash-cards and a three-question self-quiz. Hours 2 and 3 are team work, in your teams of two or three, on a defined deliverable with a template. The Binder remains individual.

  • Sprint 1 — Thursday, December 3: cyber terrorism and information warfare (Easttom Ch. 12) → Binder Part 9, the case study and the readiness memo, due Wednesday, December 9, 23:59.
  • Sprint 2 — Thursday, December 10: industrial espionage in cyberspace and e-commerce security (Ch. 7 and the PCI (Payment Card Industry) handout) → Part 10, due Wednesday, December 16, 23:59.
  • Sprint 3 — Thursday, December 17: blockchain and decentralized applications, plus the Binder integration workshop → Part 11, due Sunday, December 20, 23:59; then the Final Binder (Milestone 2), due Wednesday, January 13, 2027, 23:59.

Two rules. Questions go to the course Q&A thread — they are answered within 48 hours and consolidated at the next session. And the 2:50 exit ticket — your draft uploaded plus one line, “what I learned today” — is your attendance and participation record. The Session Packs are online one week ahead. Today's work carries straight into them: the zone design and the POS (Point of Sale) separation of Examples 1 and 2 feed Sprint 2's checkout review; the request review of Example 3 feeds its e-commerce checklist; and the traceability rules of Example 5 are exactly the rules of the Sprint 3 integration workshop and of your showcase story on January 14 — before, what we fixed first and why, after.

Real-life example 5 — The architecture review before the meeting with the CFO (Chief Financial Officer) — tracing every box to a threat

The task of the exampleA first draft of BlueFern's target architecture lists twelve controls. Before it goes to the CFO (Chief Financial Officer), check it against the four traceability rules — no orphan control, no uncovered high risk, an owner and a process for every control, numbers that agree with the risk register — find what fails, correct it, and check again until it passes.
How it relates to the lectureDefence in depth (5.1) and the four traceability rules (5.2) applied to the boxes of 5.3; the same rules govern the Sprint 3 integration workshop (5.4).

Wednesday before the CFO (Chief Financial Officer) meeting, an IT (Information Technology) staff member circulates a draft: (C1) stateful edge firewall with VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks); (C2) cloud DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet) with a WAF (Web Application Firewall); (C3) database in a private subnet; (C4) remote-access VPN (Virtual Private Network) — MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) “planned for next year”; (C5) guest SSID (Service Set Identifier) on VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) 50; (C6) EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) on laptops and servers; (C7) a SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) — no one named to read it; (C8) backups to the USB (Universal Serial Bus) drive attached to the file server; (C9) a second NGFW (Next-Generation Firewall) licence “for future use”; (C10) a password manager for the IT (Information Technology) staff only; (C11) patch management for the servers, laptops excluded; (C12) security-awareness training. The threats and risks it must answer come from the Binder: SQL (Structured Query Language) injection on the web shop (high), credential stuffing against the VPN (Virtual Private Network) (high), ransomware on the file server (high), phishing of staff passwords (high), a visitor on the Wi-Fi reaching the POS (Point of Sale) (medium), a lost unencrypted laptop with a customer export (high), an exposed MySQL database (high), an unpatched laptop exploited (medium), an insider copying the customer list (medium).

The review finds seven problems. C9 is an orphan: no threat points to it — removed. The lost laptop is uncovered — full-disk encryption and mobile device management added. Ransomware has prevention and detection but no working recovery, because C8's drive is attached and would be encrypted too — an offline, immutable copy and a monthly restore test added. Credential stuffing against the VPN (Virtual Private Network) has no real prevention while MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) waits for next year — MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) moved to now. C7 has no owner — one IT (Information Technology) staff member named, a weekly review, and alerts routed by e-mail or to a managed service. C11 leaves the laptops, and the medium risk of an exploited laptop, half-covered — EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) would detect the exploitation, but nothing prevents it — so the laptops are added to patch management. The insider risk has detection only (C7) — noted, and carried to Sprint 2, where data-loss prevention and the leaver procedure are studied. Numbers: EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) plus MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) on the customer database costs $30,000 per year and lowers the annualized loss from $100,000 to $20,000 — the Class 6 arithmetic — so the net benefit of $50,000 goes into the summary for the CFO (Chief Financial Officer).

Deliverable and where it goes next. The traceability matrix template and the findings list (downloadable below) are the tools for the control-to-threat table of Exercise 10.1: run your own table through the same four rules before you submit Part 8. In Research Sprint 3, the integration workshop applies exactly these rules to the whole Binder (Appendix B: every control in Part 8 points to a threat in Part 3 or a risk in Part 6; the numbers agree), and the before/after graph is the middle slide of your showcase story.

Interactive example 5 — Traceability checker — controls ↔ threats

The task of the programThe program loads the draft architecture (twelve controls with their type, owner and mapped threats) and the nine threats with their risk level, and checks the four rules one at a time: orphan controls, uncovered high risks, missing owners or processes, and a cost-benefit check against the risk register. It draws the controls and threats as two columns joined by coloured lines (prevent, detect, recover), marks every failure, prints the findings, then applies the reviewer's corrections and checks again.
How it relates to the lectureDefence in depth (5.1), the four traceability rules (5.2) and the components of the diagram (5.3); the rules are those of Appendix B used in the Sprint 3 integration workshop (5.4).

File: CS474_Class10_Example5_traceability_checker.html — self-contained HTML; a comment before every line of code; Copy · Start / Pause · Step · Restart · downloads; execution window; visualization.

Step by step — how the program works
  1. Press Start. The draft appears: twelve controls on the left, nine threats on the right, one line per mapping, coloured by type — teal prevents, amber detects, blue recovers.
  2. Rule 1 checks every control for at least one mapped threat; an orphan control turns yellow and a finding is printed.
  3. Rule 2 checks every high threat for at least one preventive and one detective-or-recovery control; an uncovered threat turns red, a half-covered one amber.
  4. Rule 3 checks every control for an owner and a process; a control without one gets a warning mark.
  5. Rule 4 compares the annual cost of each costed control with the reduction of annualized loss it claims (Class 6 arithmetic) and prints the net benefit.
  6. The review step applies the corrections one by one — remove the orphan, add disk encryption, add the offline backup and restore test, move MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) to now, name the SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) owner, extend patching — and the checks run again until every line is green.
  7. Press Pause at any step; Step advances one check; Restart reloads the draft. Download saves the traceability matrix and the findings (CSV (Comma-Separated Values)) and the graph (PNG (Portable Network Graphics)); Copy copies the whole program.

Five flash-cards — click a card to reveal its back

What is defence in depth?
click to reveal ↻
Several independent layers of control — people, process and technology — so that the failure of one layer does not become a breach. Today's layers: zones and firewalls, remote and wireless access, the application, endpoint and central software, and recovery.
What is a target architecture, and which two documents make it up?
click to reveal ↻
The planned state of the company's systems: a diagram with each control placed where it acts, and a control-to-threat table that links every control to the threats or risks it addresses.
State the four traceability rules.
click to reveal ↻
1) No orphan control — each control points to a threat (Part 3) or a risk (Part 6). 2) No uncovered high risk — at least one preventive and one detective or recovery control. 3) Every control has an owner and a process. 4) The numbers agree across Parts 1, 6 and 8.
Zero trust in one sentence.
click to reveal ↻
No request is trusted because of the network it comes from; every access is authenticated and authorized, the device is checked, privileges are minimal, and everything is monitored (NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-207).
How does a Research Sprint run?
click to reveal ↻
Hour 1: guided self-study from the Session Pack on the LMS (Learning Management System) (reading guide, short recorded mini-lecture, flash-cards, self-quiz). Hours 2–3: team work on a defined deliverable with a template. Questions to the Q&A thread (answered within 48 hours). The 2:50 exit ticket records attendance and participation.

Quiz — 4 MCQ + 2 MSQ

📝 FORMATIVE QUIZ — this quiz is not summative: it does not count toward your final grade. Nothing is recorded; use it to check your understanding.

Q1 · MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) A draft architecture includes a second NGFW (Next-Generation Firewall) licence “for future use”, mapped to no threat. Under the traceability rules, this control is:

  1. Wrong — “uncovered” describes a threat without controls, not a control without threats.
  2. Wrong — every control must be justified by a threat or risk.
  3. Wrong — nothing in the draft says it restores anything.
  4. Correct — no threat points to it, so it is cost without demonstrated benefit.
Hint: Rule 1.

Q2 · MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) The SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) collects every log, but nobody is assigned to read its alerts. Which rule fails?

  1. Correct — without an owner and a routine, the alerts are never acted upon.
  2. Wrong — the SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) does point to threats.
  3. Wrong — nothing here concerns costs or values.
  4. Wrong — the question is about the control's operation, not about a threat's coverage.
Hint: Lesson 4: a SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) nobody reads is not a control.

Q3 · MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) BlueFern's backups go to a USB (Universal Serial Bus) drive permanently attached to the file server. For the ransomware risk, what is missing?

  1. Wrong — a firewall does not restore files.
  2. Wrong — a WAF (Web Application Firewall) protects the web application.
  3. Correct — an attached drive is encrypted with the server; recovery needs an offline or immutable copy that has been tested.
  4. Wrong — guest separation addresses a different threat.
Hint: Rule 2 — prevention, detection, and what else for a high risk?

Q4 · MCQ (Multiple-Choice Question) During a Research Sprint, you have a question about the content. What do you do?

  1. Wrong — questions are answered within 48 hours and consolidated at the next session.
  2. Correct — this is the designed process.
  3. Wrong — the exit ticket is your attendance and participation record.
  4. Wrong — the Binder is individual work (academic integrity).
Hint: Section 5.4 — the first of the two rules.

Q5 · MSQ (Multiple-Select Question) (3 correct answers) Which elements belong in BlueFern's target architecture (the Exercise 10.1 list)?

  1. Correct — guest Wi-Fi isolation is on the list.
  2. Correct — the DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet) and the WAF (Web Application Firewall) are on the list.
  3. Wrong — the database moves to a private subnet.
  4. Wrong — FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is removed (security misconfiguration).
  5. Correct — the VPN (Virtual Private Network) with MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) is on the list.
  6. Wrong — shared passwords are replaced by individual accounts, MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) and a password manager.
Hint: Section 5.3.

Q6 · MSQ (Multiple-Select Question) (2 correct answers) Which statements about the Research Sprints are correct?

  1. Wrong — they are scheduled sessions of the course.
  2. Correct — draft uploaded plus one line.
  3. Wrong — Parts 9, 10 and 11 are due on December 9, 16 and 20.
  4. Wrong — it records attendance and participation.
  5. Correct — reading guide, mini-lecture, flash-cards, self-quiz.
  6. Wrong — within 48 hours, in the Q&A thread.
Hint: Section 5.4 — the shape of the session and the two rules.

Hours 2–3 and the Binder — summary only

After the break, the three exercises of Binder Part 8 are worked in teams of two or three; every student submits an individual Binder. They are only summarized here — the exercise sheets and templates are handed out separately in class.

  • Exercise 10.1 — Target architecture. A diagram of BlueFern after the changes — firewall, DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet) for the web shop, VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks), VPN (Virtual Private Network) with MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication), guest Wi-Fi isolation, WAF (Web Application Firewall), EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response), SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) or log collector, backups — and a control-to-threat table that links each control to the threats of Part 3 and the risks of Part 6. Lessons 1, 2 and 5 and Examples 1, 2 and 5 give you the method: zones and rules, SSIDs (Service Set Identifiers) and VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks), and the four traceability rules.
  • Exercise 10.2 — Web-shop security checklist and the vulnerable snippet. Twelve checklist items based on the OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) Top 10 for shop.bluefern.example, and the correction of the vulnerable login snippet: parameterized query, output encoding and hashed-password comparison. Lesson 3, its practical and Example 3 show the method on different requests.
  • Exercise 10.3 — Security-software selection matrix. Five categories × what each protects, what it misses, its cost class, the effort to run it, and your pick for BlueFern. Lesson 4 and Example 4 show the reasoning on one intrusion.
  • Last 15 minutes — Sprint briefing. Teams confirmed, Session Packs on the LMS (Learning Management System), the Q&A thread, the exit-ticket rule, and the deliverables and dates of December 3, 10 and 17.

All links used, with a short explanation

Every link points to the official website of the organization or document named, and every one was opened on November 14, 2026. Before clicking any link, check it with VirusTotal and Google Safe Browsing (Legal Notice, Annex C).

Firewalls, segmentation and network architecture

  • NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1 — Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy (2009) — NIST — The reference guide to firewall technologies (packet filtering, stateful inspection, application firewalls), firewall policy and the placement of firewalls and a DMZ (Demilitarized Zone — also called a screened subnet). (Lesson 1) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing
  • NIST SP 800-215 — Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape (2022) — NIST — How enterprise networks are secured today: segmentation, secure remote access, cloud and zero trust — the landscape of Lessons 1, 2 and 5. (Lessons 1, 2, 5) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing
  • NIST SP 800-207 — Zero Trust Architecture (2020) — NIST — Defines zero trust: no implicit trust from network location; every access request is authenticated, authorized and checked against the device's state. (Lessons 1, 5) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing
  • Canadian Centre for Cyber Security — Network security zoning (ITSG-38) — Canadian Centre for Cyber Security — The Canadian zone model — Public Zone, Public Access Zone, Operations Zone, Restricted Zone — and where to place each service. (Lesson 1) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing
  • IEEE 802.1 Working Group (802.1Q bridges and VLANs; 802.1X port-based network access control) — IEEE — The standards body behind VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) tagging (802.1Q) and port-based access control (802.1X) used on switches and enterprise Wi-Fi. (Lessons 1, 2) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing
  • OWASP CRS — the Core Rule Set for web application firewalls — OWASP CRS Project — The open attack-detection rule set used by ModSecurity, Coraza and compatible WAF (Web Application Firewall) engines. (Lesson 1) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing

Remote access and wireless

  • NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1 — Guide to IPsec VPNs (2020) — NIST — How IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) VPNs (Virtual Private Networks) work (IKE (Internet Key Exchange), ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload), tunnel mode) and how to plan and deploy them for sites and remote users. (Lesson 2) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing
  • Canadian Centre for Cyber Security — Virtual private networks (ITSAP.80.101) — Canadian Centre for Cyber Security — Activate MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) with phishing-resistant factors, keep the VPN (Virtual Private Network) patched, and avoid split tunnelling where possible. (Lesson 2) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing

  • Wi-Fi Alliance — Security (WPA3, Wi-Fi Enhanced Open) — Wi-Fi Alliance — WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3) Personal and Enterprise, Protected Management Frames, Wi-Fi Enhanced Open; WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3) is mandatory for Wi-Fi CERTIFIED devices. (Lesson 2) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing
  • NIST SP 800-63B-4 — Authentication and Authenticator Management (2025) — NIST — The current United States guideline for authenticators, MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) and password rules (including checks against breached passwords). (Lessons 2, 3) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing

Web-application security

  • OWASP Top 10:2025 — the ten most critical web application security risks — OWASP — The 2025 edition: A01 Broken Access Control, A02 Security Misconfiguration, A03 Software Supply Chain Failures, A04 Cryptographic Failures, A05 Injection, A06 Insecure Design, A07 Authentication Failures, A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures, A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures, A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions. (Lesson 3) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing
  • OWASP Top 10:2025 — A05 Injection — OWASP — The injection category, which includes SQL (Structured Query Language) injection and cross-site scripting. (Lesson 3) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing
  • OWASP Top 10:2025 — A07 Authentication Failures — OWASP — Credential stuffing, brute force, weak passwords, missing MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) and weak session management. (Lesson 3) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing
  • OWASP Top 10:2025 — A02 Security Misconfiguration — OWASP — Default accounts, unnecessary features, verbose errors and missing hardening — second place in 2025. (Lesson 3) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing
  • OWASP Cheat Sheet — SQL Injection Prevention — OWASP — Primary defences: parameterized queries and allow-list input validation; manual escaping is strongly discouraged. (Lesson 3) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing
  • OWASP Cheat Sheet — Cross Site Scripting Prevention — OWASP — Context-aware output encoding, HTML (HyperText Markup Language) sanitization, safe framework use, and CSP (Content Security Policy) as defence in depth. (Lesson 3) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing
  • OWASP Cheat Sheet — Session Management — OWASP — Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite cookie attributes, the __Host- prefix, and renewing the session ID (Identifier) after login. (Lesson 3) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing
  • RFC 6797 — HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) — IETF / RFC Editor — The standard behind the Strict-Transport-Security header: the browser uses only HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) for the site for a stated period. (Lesson 3) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing
  • RFC 6265 — HTTP State Management Mechanism (cookies) — IETF / RFC Editor — The cookie standard (Secure and HttpOnly attributes); its revision, RFC (Request for Comments — an Internet standards document) 6265bis, adds SameSite and is still an Internet-Draft. (Lesson 3) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing

Security software and patching

  • NIST SP 800-83 Rev. 1 — Guide to Malware Incident Prevention and Handling for Desktops and Laptops — NIST — What antivirus and related tools can and cannot do, and how malware incidents are prevented and handled. (Lesson 4) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing
  • NIST SP 800-94 — Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems — NIST — IDS (Intrusion Detection System) and IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) types and detection methods (Class 6), reused here as one of the security-software families. (Lesson 4) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing
  • NIST SP 800-40 Rev. 4 — Guide to Enterprise Patch Management Planning (2022) — NIST — Patching treated as preventive maintenance: an enterprise strategy that makes updates routine and reduces risk. (Lesson 4) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing
  • Canadian Centre for Cyber Security — Password managers: Security tips (ITSAP.30.025) — Canadian Centre for Cyber Security — Benefits of password managers and their main risk — compromise of all accounts at once — with the protections: strong primary passphrase and MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication). (Lesson 4) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing
  • Canadian Centre for Cyber Security — Baseline cyber security controls for small and medium organizations — Canadian Centre for Cyber Security — Thirteen baseline controls for organizations the size of BlueFern: patching, security software, strong authentication, perimeter defences, secure websites, backups and more. (Lessons 4, 5) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing
  • CIS Critical Security Controls Version 8.1 — CIS — A prioritized list of security controls with implementation groups for small and larger organizations. (Lesson 5) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing
  • PCI Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) — PCI Security Standards Council — The payment-card standard (version 4.x): network security controls, protection of public-facing web applications, MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) — Research Sprint 2 material. (Lessons 1, 5) · check: VirusTotal · Safe Browsing

Full text: Cyber.SoHo — Legal Notice, Terms of Use and Acceptable Use Policy (v2.0). It applies to all Cyber.SoHo materials, including this computer-security module. The sections that apply here:

2 (scope and acceptance — using this module means accepting the Notice); 4.2 and 4.3 (licence and restrictions — no copying, no re-posting, no recording and no use as training data for any machine-learning system); 4.4 and 4.6 (trademarks and third-party content — OWASP, NIST, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, the Wi-Fi Alliance, the PCI Security Standards Council, the textbook and the linked Professor Messer videos are cited with attribution); 5 (no affiliation with any vendor, platform, publisher or channel linked here); 6 (acceptable use — authorization governs everything; 6.3 forbids scanning, probing or capturing traffic on any network or website outside your authorized lab); 7.2 (monitoring and capture — never put a wireless card in monitor mode on a network you share with other people); 7.4 (defensive tooling and configuration changes — firewall rules, blocking and quarantine actions can cut off legitimate users; never apply them to a live system without the owner's written approval, an agreed change window and a tested rollback); 7.6 (scanning is an intrusive act — designated targets only); 8 (legal warning — Criminal Code of Canada s. 342.1, s. 184 and s. 430(1.1)); 11 (disclaimer — links and videos were checked on November 14, 2026 and may change); 14 and Annex C (external links and downloads — check every link with VirusTotal and Google Safe Browsing before you click); 17 (no recording of sessions); 18 (academic integrity — your Binder is your own work); 20 (personal information); Annex A (the e-signature acknowledgement form, provided as a separate file); Annex D (written authorization template).

Legal & Ethical Notice of the course schedule — read before any lab. All scanning, testing and “attack” exercises in this course are performed exclusively on the lab systems and the fictional BlueFern Trading Inc. scenario provided, with explicit authorization. Unauthorized access to, or interference with, computer systems is a criminal offence — for example under the Canadian Criminal Code s. 342.1, the United States Computer Fraud and Abuse Act 18 U.S.C. § 1030, EU (European Union) Directive 2013/40/EU and Spain's Ley Orgánica 10/1995 — regardless of intent. Never test a system you do not own or do not have written permission to test. No OSINT (Open-Source Intelligence) on real people or real organizations is ever part of this course. The five simulators of this module run entirely inside your browser: they send no packets, scan nothing and contact no website. Typing an injection string into a real website, or surveying a Wi-Fi network you do not own, is not a course activity.
